Testosterone replacement is the mainstay (virilisation, muscle/bone, libido — but does NOT restore fertility); sperm retrieval (micro-TESE) + ICSI can achieve fatherhood in some (discuss before testosterone therapy); manage gynaecomastia, osteoporosis, metabolic risk; genetic counselling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the defining triad of haemolytic uraemic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (a thrombotic microangiopathy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the commonest cause of acute kidney injury in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Which organism classically precedes typical HUS, and via what toxin?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) — Shiga toxin. (Shigella can also cause it.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Describe the core mechanism of HUS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Shiga toxin damages vascular endothelium (especially renal microvasculature) → platelet activation and microthrombi in small vessels (thrombotic microangiopathy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does the HUS mechanism explain each part of the triad?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: MAHA — red cells sheared through clogged microvasculature (schistocytes); thrombocytopenia — platelets consumed in microthrombi; AKI — microthrombi occlude the glomerular microvasculature.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Typical vs atypical HUS — frequency and trigger?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical (STEC-HUS/D+HUS) ~90%, triggered by Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhoea. Atypical (aHUS) ~10%, complement (alternative-pathway) dysregulation, often no diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does treatment differ between typical and atypical HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical STEC-HUS: supportive. Atypical HUS: eculizumab (anti-C5).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does prognosis differ between typical and atypical HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Typical usually recovers; atypical has a worse, often relapsing course.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Name a further recognised form of HUS beyond STEC and complement-mediated.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Streptococcus pneumoniae-associated HUS (~5–15%, e.g. after invasive pneumococcal disease/pneumonia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Describe the typical prodrome of STEC-HUS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: A diarrhoeal illness — classically BLOODY diarrhoea (haemorrhagic colitis), abdominal pain, vomiting — from undercooked beef, unpasteurised milk, petting farms, or person-to-person spread.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How long after diarrhoea onset does STEC-HUS typically develop, and in what proportion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: ~5–14 days after the diarrhoea starts, in ~10–15% of infected children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What clinical features appear when the HUS triad develops?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Anaemia (pallor, lethargy, jaundice); thrombocytopenia (bruising, petechiae, bleeding); AKI (reduced urine output/oliguria-anuria, oedema, hypertension, rising creatinine).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What extra-renal complications occur in severe HUS (~20%)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: CNS involvement (irritability, seizures, encephalopathy — worse prognosis), cardiac, and pancreatic (glucose) involvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What blood film and FBC findings are expected in HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Anaemia with schistocytes (fragmented RBCs), thrombocytopenia, reticulocytosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What haemolysis screen findings are seen in HUS, and what is the Coombs result?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: ↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, and a NEGATIVE Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test — non-immune haemolysis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Why is the coagulation screen important in suspected HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: It is NORMAL in HUS — the key distinction from DIC, where it is deranged.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What stool tests are used in suspected STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Stool culture / PCR for STEC / E. coli O157 and Shiga toxin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How does TTP differ from HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: TTP is a pentad (MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI + neurological signs + fever), caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency; more neuro/less renal, adults > children; treated with plasma exchange.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: How is DIC distinguished from HUS on labs?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: HUS has a NORMAL coagulation screen; DIC is deranged — ↑PT/APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the mainstay of management for STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Supportive care — there is no specific treatment; most children recover. Careful fluid/electrolyte management, BP control, nutrition.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: When are blood and platelet transfusions used in HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Blood transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; platelets are generally AVOIDED unless active bleeding/surgery (can fuel microthrombi).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What proportion of HUS children need dialysis, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: ~50% — for AKI, hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or uraemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: Which agents must be AVOIDED in suspected STEC-HUS and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Antibiotics and anti-motility/antidiarrhoeal agents — they increase Shiga toxin release/absorption and the risk of HUS.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the treatment for atypical (complement-mediated) HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Eculizumab (anti-C5 monoclonal antibody) — has transformed its outcome; also used in some centres for severe STEC-HUS with CNS involvement.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What public health action is required in STEC/E. coli O157 HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Notify (it is a notifiable organism) and undertake source tracing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.front: What is the prognosis of STEC-HUS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Haemolytic Urae.back: Acute mortality now <5%; most recover, but ~1/3 have long-term renal sequelae (CKD, hypertension, proteinuria) → long-term renal follow-up. CNS involvement worsens outcome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: An acquired autoimmune disorder in which antibodies destroy platelets, causing isolated thrombocytopenia with bruising and a petechial/purpuric rash.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the commonest cause of acute-onset thrombocytopenia in an otherwise-well child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the key management principle in childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Treat the BLEEDING, not the platelet number — most children need only watchful waiting, not treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Describe the core mechanism of ITP.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Antibodies against the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex → type II hypersensitivity → antibody-coated platelets destroyed by the spleen (± impaired production).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What typically triggers acute childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: It is typically acute and post-viral — often 1–2 weeks after a viral infection (or, less often, vaccination); a transient immune response, which is why it usually resolves.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Why is ITP described as a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: The assessment confirms isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child and excludes marrow failure/malignancy (leukaemia, aplastic anaemia); there is no confirmatory test.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Which features on other cell lines reassure you it is ITP rather than leukaemia/aplastic anaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Normal Hb and WCC (isolated ↓platelets). Anaemia or abnormal WCC (pancytopenia) is a red flag.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What systemic and examination red flags suggest a sinister cause rather than ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Fever, weight loss, bone pain, malaise; lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. In ITP the child is well with no organomegaly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What blood film finding would point away from ITP toward malignancy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Blasts or abnormal cells. In ITP the film is normal apart from few (often large/young) platelets.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: If a red flag is present, what must be done before giving steroids and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bone marrow examination to exclude leukaemia — steroids could partially treat/mask leukaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the classic age range for childhood ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: 2–7 years, often 1–2 weeks after a viral illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What are the typical skin findings in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bruising (ecchymoses) and a petechial or purpuric rash — non-blanching, often on the legs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What types of bleeding occur in ITP, and which marks higher risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Bleeding is less common — typically epistaxis or gingival (gum) bleeding; mucosal bleeding ('wet purpura') is a marker of higher bleeding risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How common is serious bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Rare — intracranial haemorrhage occurs in <0.5%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the central FBC pattern in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Isolated thrombocytopenia — normal haemoglobin and white cell count.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What does the blood film help exclude in suspected ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Blasts (leukaemia), fragments (HUS/TTP), and pseudothrombocytopenia (platelet clumping); it confirms low platelets, often large/young.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When is bone marrow examination indicated in suspected ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Only if atypical: lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, failure to respond to treatment, abnormal other cell lines, or before starting steroids if leukaemia is a concern.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Is anti-platelet antibody testing routine in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: No — ITP is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion with no confirmatory test; anti-platelet antibody testing is not routine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How is ITP classified by duration?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Newly diagnosed: <3 months; persistent: 3–12 months; chronic: >12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What proportion of children develop chronic ITP, and who is more at risk?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: ~20–30%; more likely in older children/adolescents, insidious onset, and girls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is first-line management for most children with ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Watchful waiting — for no or only minor bleeding (bruising/petechiae only), regardless of how low the count is; ~80% resolve spontaneously within ~6 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What safety advice is given during watchful waiting for ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Avoid contact sports and trauma; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin and IM injections; written safety-net; return if significant bleeding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the first-line drug treatment when there is significant/mucosal bleeding?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) — a short course, reducing platelet destruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When is IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) used in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: When a faster rise is needed (active bleeding, before a procedure), or if steroids are unsuitable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is a role for IV anti-D immunoglobulin in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: An alternative in Rh-positive, non-splenectomised children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: When are platelet transfusions used in ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Only for life-threatening bleeding — transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed too, so they are used with IVIG/steroids as rescue, not routinely.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: How is life-threatening bleeding (e.g. intracranial haemorrhage) in ITP managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Combination rescue: platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG (± tranexamic acid; emergency splenectomy as last resort).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What are the second-line options for chronic/refractory ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim); rituximab; splenectomy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: Why is splenectomy generally deferred/avoided in children with ITP?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: High spontaneous-resolution rate plus infection risk — reserved for chronic, refractory disease, usually age >5.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.front: What is the key differential of ITP and its red flags?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Immune Thromboc.back: Acute leukaemia — red flags: unwell child, other cytopenias, organomegaly, bone pain.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What two common feeding-related presentations are grouped under infant feeding & reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA) and gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR/GORD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the organising principle distinguishing benign from concerning infant feeding presentations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Physiological reflux (posseting, otherwise thriving) usually resolves by ~1 year; red flags (poor weight gain, distress, blood) suggest GORD or CMPA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What clues point to cow's milk protein intolerance, and how is it managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Vomiting, diarrhoea/blood in stool, eczema, poor weight gain → exclude cow's milk (extensively hydrolysed formula / maternal dairy exclusion).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How do you distinguish infant reflux GOR from GORD, and how is each managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR = effortless posseting → reassure. GORD = distress/faltering growth → thickened feeds, alginates, PPI.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should reflux be treated as GORD rather than simple posseting?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: When there is faltering growth, marked distress, haematemesis, or respiratory symptoms — investigate/treat; consider CMPA in refractory reflux + atopy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: An immune-mediated adverse reaction to the proteins in cow's milk (mainly casein and whey); one of the commonest food allergies of infancy (~1–3% of infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is CMPA both over- and under-diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Its GI, skin and respiratory symptoms overlap with reflux, colic and infection, and there is no single confirmatory test for non-IgE disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How does 'allergy' differ from 'intolerance' in this context?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Allergy = immune-mediated (IgE or non-IgE) — what CMPA refers to. True intolerance is non-immune (e.g. lactose intolerance — an enzyme/sugar problem), a completely different entity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the timing of IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA reactions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: <2 hours after ingestion (immediate). Non-IgE-mediated: after 4 hours, up to 24–48 h/days (delayed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the mechanism of IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: immediate hypersensitivity (mast cell/IgE). Non-IgE-mediated: cell-mediated (delayed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the typical features of IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Urticaria, wheeze, stridor, angioedema; acute; can progress to anaphylaxis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the typical features of non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Rectal bleeding, mucus in stool, vomiting, diarrhoea; GI-predominant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What testing helps in IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: skin prick / specific IgE (RAST) helpful. Non-IgE-mediated: no useful blood test — diagnosis is clinical (elimination + reintroduction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When do IgE-mediated vs non-IgE-mediated CMPA typically resolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: IgE-mediated: later, ~by 5 years. Non-IgE-mediated: earlier, ~by 3 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When and in whom does CMPA usually present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Usually in the first 3 months of life, in formula-fed infants — but can occur in exclusively breastfed babies from maternal dairy passing into breast milk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List the GI features of CMPA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Regurgitation/vomiting, diarrhoea, colic (irritability, crying), rectal bleeding/mucus (non-IgE), constipation, faltering growth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List the skin and respiratory features of CMPA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Skin: urticaria, atopic eczema, angioedema. Respiratory: wheeze, chronic cough, stridor (IgE). Anaphylaxis is rare but possible in IgE-mediated disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the cornerstone of diagnosing CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: It is primarily clinical — improvement on removing cow's milk protein and recurrence on reintroduction (especially for non-IgE disease where tests don't help).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which unproven test should be avoided in CMPA and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Food-specific IgG panels — not validated, cause overdiagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the first-line formula for mild–moderate CMPA in a formula-fed infant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Extensively Hydrolysed Formula (EHF) — cow's-milk protein broken down so it's not recognised; tolerated by ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When is Amino Acid Formula (AAF) used in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: If severe, or no response to EHF — fully non-allergenic; only ~10% of infants need it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which milks/formulas should NOT be used in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Soya formula (cross-reactivity, especially <6 months) or other mammalian milks (goat/sheep — cross-react).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is CMPA managed in a breastfed infant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Continue breastfeeding; eliminate cow's milk protein from the maternal diet and give the mother calcium (± vitamin D). When breastfeeding stops, use EHF.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How long is EHF continued after breastfeeding stops in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Until ~12 months of age and for at least 6 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is dietitian involvement important in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: To ensure nutritional adequacy (calcium/vitamin D), avoid hidden allergens, and prevent unnecessary long-term restriction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the 'milk ladder' in CMPA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Planned staged reintroduction starting with small amounts of BAKED milk (e.g. malted-milk biscuit) → progressing up, to confirm resolution and build tolerance (supervised/specialist for IgE-mediated).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should a child with CMPA be referred to paediatrics/allergy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: If severe — failure to thrive, anaphylaxis, or severe symptoms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR) in babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: The passage of stomach contents up into the oesophagus — effortless posseting/regurgitation of milk after feeds; extremely common and physiological (≥40% of infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is physiological GOR in a thriving baby managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Reassurance only, not treatment — it is often over-medicalised.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Why is reflux so common in babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Short narrow oesophagus, relatively incompetent/immature lower oesophageal sphincter, large fluid milk volume, and much time lying flat → milk easily flows back up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When does physiological GOR usually resolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: As the baby matures, sits up and takes solids — ~90% by 12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How does GOR differ from GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR is normal, effortless regurgitation in a well, thriving 'happy spitter'. GORD is reflux causing symptoms/complications in a distressed, unwell or faltering baby.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the key teaching point about GOR and crying?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: GOR does NOT cause crying/irritability in an otherwise healthy, thriving infant — if a baby is genuinely distressed or not growing, think GORD or an alternative diagnosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What are the clinical features of GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Regurgitation/vomiting WITH poor weight gain, feeding difficulties (refusal, pulling off, distress/pain), marked unexplained irritability (especially with arching), Sandifer syndrome, respiratory symptoms and oesophagitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is Sandifer syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Episodic dystonic posturing — torticollis (neck twisting) + back arching — associated with GORD; can be mistaken for seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What respiratory and oesophageal complications can GORD cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Chronic cough, wheeze (aspiration), recurrent chest infections, apnoea/BRUE; oesophagitis (haematemesis, pain), dental erosion in older children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Which vomiting red flag suggests intestinal obstruction and needs urgent surgical referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Bilious (green) vomiting → intestinal obstruction (e.g. malrotation/volvulus) — urgent, same-day surgical referral. Never ignore green vomit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What does projectile, non-bilious vomiting in a 2–8-week-old suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Pyloric stenosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: List reflux red flags that mean 'not simple reflux — investigate/refer'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Bilious vomiting, projectile non-bilious vomiting (2–8 wks), haematemesis/melaena, abdominal distension/tenderness, bulging fontanelle/altered consciousness, blood in stool, onset after 6 months or persisting beyond 1 year, fever/lethargy, faltering growth, chronic diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What should prompt consideration of CMPA in a baby with reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Eczema, family history of atopy, or other GI symptoms — CMPA can present as/with reflux.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: Is GORD usually diagnosed clinically or with investigations?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Usually a clinical diagnosis — investigations are rarely needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What investigations may be considered in GORD, and when?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Urinalysis (exclude UTI if faltering growth/late onset); and only if diagnostic doubt/complications/red flags: pH/impedance monitoring, upper GI endoscopy (suspected oesophagitis), contrast study (if anatomical/obstruction suspected).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the first step of stepped-care management (NICE NG1) for reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Feeding review — assess technique/volume, avoid overfeeding (smaller, more frequent feeds); breastfeeding assessment if breastfed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the stepped-care approach for a breastfed infant with troublesome reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Breastfeeding assessment → if it persists, a trial of alginate (Gaviscon Infant) for 1–2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the stepped-care approach for a formula-fed infant with troublesome reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Review feed volumes → thickened (anti-reflux) formula → if unsuccessful, stop thickener and trial alginate for 1–2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When should acid suppression (PPI/H2RA) be offered in infant reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: NOT for overt regurgitation alone in an otherwise-well infant. Consider a PPI (or H2RA) trial only for unexplained feeding difficulties, distressed behaviour, or faltering growth with suspected acid reflux/oesophagitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: How is endoscopy-proven reflux oesophagitis treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: PPI/H2RA treatment. Do NOT use prokinetics (metoclopramide/domperidone/erythromycin) without specialist advice.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: When is specialist referral / fundoplication considered for GORD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: For severe, intractable GORD unresponsive to medical treatment, or complications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.front: What is the safe-sleep caveat when managing infant reflux?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Infant Feeding.back: Do NOT use positional (head-up/prone/side) management to treat reflux in sleeping infants — babies must be placed on their BACK to sleep (SIDS prevention overrides reflux positioning).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What three conditions are grouped under lower respiratory infection & wheeze in young children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Bronchiolitis, whooping cough (pertussis), and viral-induced (pre-school) wheeze.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the organising principle for these conditions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Age + pattern: bronchiolitis <1yr (RSV coryza → cough/wheeze/feeding difficulty); pertussis = paroxysmal cough + whoop/apnoea + post-tussive vomiting; viral-induced wheeze = episodic wheeze with viral URTIs and no interval symptoms (not asthma).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: <1yr, RSV; coryza then wheeze/crackles, poor feeding → supportive (oxygen, feeding support); admit if severe/apnoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, apnoea in infants, post-tussive vomiting → macrolide; notifiable; vaccine-preventable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Give the clue and management for pre-school/viral-induced wheeze.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Episodic wheeze with viral URTI, well between episodes → SABA; distinguish from asthma (atopy, interval symptoms).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: An acute viral lower respiratory tract infection of the small airways (bronchioles) in infants, causing inflammation, mucus and airway obstruction → coryza then cough, wheeze/crackles and feeding difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does bronchiolitis matter clinically?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is the commonest LRTI and commonest cause of hospital admission in infants under 1 year; RSV is the main cause; and management is a 'less is more' point — it is supportive (bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics don't work).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the core mechanism of bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A virus (usually RSV) infects and inflames the bronchiolar epithelium → oedema, mucus and sloughed cells plug the tiny airways; because infant airways are small, minor narrowing causes big obstruction → air trapping/hyperinflation, wheeze, crackles, work of breathing → feeding difficulty and, in the youngest, apnoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What organism causes most cases of bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) — ~70–85% of cases; others include parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, influenza, adenovirus, rhinovirus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the typical age and season for bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Under 2 years, peak ~3–6 months; winter epidemics; spread by droplets/contact (very contagious).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis distinguished from viral-induced wheeze/asthma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Bronchiolitis: <1–2 yrs, widespread crackles ± wheeze, low-grade fever, first episode with coryzal prodrome. Viral wheeze/asthma: usually >1 yr, wheeze without crackles, recurrent, atopy/family history (both unusual under 1 year).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis distinguished from pneumonia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Pneumonia has focal crackles, high/persistent fever (>39°C) and persistent focal signs; bronchiolitis has widespread crackles and low-grade fever. High fever or focal crackles → think pneumonia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the typical clinical course of bronchiolitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Coryzal prodrome (runny nose, mild fever) for 1–3 days, then persistent cough, tachypnoea and increased work of breathing (recession, nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting), wheeze and/or fine bibasal crackles, and feeding difficulty. Signs peak days 3–5 then improve; cough can linger ~3 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why is feeding difficulty important in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is a key marker of severity (from respiratory effort/nasal blockage) and guides admission.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is a crucial, potentially life-threatening presenting feature of bronchiolitis in young/preterm infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Apnoea — especially in infants <6 weeks/preterm; it may be the presenting feature and is life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is bronchiolitis diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is a CLINICAL diagnosis — do NOT routinely do blood tests or a chest X-ray (CXR can mimic pneumonia → unnecessary antibiotics).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the role of pulse oximetry and nasopharyngeal aspirate in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Pulse oximetry — for hypoxia, guides admission. Nasopharyngeal aspirate/viral PCR (RSV) — mainly for cohorting/infection control, not diagnosis. Capillary blood gas only if severe/impending respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the mainstay of bronchiolitis management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Supportive care (NICE NG9) — most are managed at home.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What oxygen thresholds guide supplemental O2 in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Give supplemental O2 if SpO2 <90% in children ≥6 weeks (or <92% if <6 weeks/comorbid).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What feeding/fluid support is used in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Smaller/more frequent feeds; nasogastric/orogastric or IV fluids if not feeding adequately; nasal suctioning if secretions/apnoea; minimal handling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is respiratory failure escalated in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: High-flow humidified oxygen (Optiflow)/CPAP → ventilation for respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Which treatments do NOT work in bronchiolitis and should not be used routinely?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Bronchodilators (salbutamol), nebulised adrenaline, corticosteroids, nebulised hypertonic saline, montelukast and antibiotics. (Antibiotics only if genuine evidence of secondary bacterial infection.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features warrant immediate emergency referral to hospital in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Apnoea, looks seriously unwell, severe respiratory distress (grunting, marked recession, RR >70), central cyanosis, or SpO2 persistently <92% in air.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features should prompt considering referral in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: RR >60, difficulty feeding/inadequate oral intake (50–75% of normal), clinical dehydration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Which risk factors lower the threshold for admission in bronchiolitis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Age <3 months, prematurity (especially <32 weeks), chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency, neuromuscular disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is nirsevimab and its role in RSV prevention?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A long-acting anti-RSV monoclonal antibody; a single injection lasts the RSV season and (unlike palivizumab) is used in healthy term/late-preterm infants; being rolled out in national programmes (UK from 2024–25). Palivizumab (monthly, high-risk only) is being phased out.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What other RSV prevention measure is part of the new UK programme?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Maternal RSV vaccination (given in pregnancy to protect the newborn); plus general measures — breastfeeding, hand hygiene, avoiding smoke exposure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is pertussis and what causes it?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A highly contagious bacterial respiratory infection caused by Bordetella pertussis (a Gram-negative coccobacillus), characterised by a prolonged paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory 'whoop'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does pertussis matter now?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Despite being vaccine-preventable it is resurgent (major UK/global outbreaks from 2024); it is most dangerous in young infants (<6 months) causing apnoea, pneumonia and death; prevention hinges on maternal vaccination in pregnancy; and it is notifiable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the core mechanism of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: B. pertussis infects the ciliated respiratory epithelium and releases toxins (pertussis toxin) that paralyse mucociliary clearance → mucus accumulates and can't be cleared → the violent repetitive coughing paroxysms (the '100-day cough').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the three stages of pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Catarrhal (~1–2 weeks), paroxysmal (~2–6 weeks), convalescent (weeks–months).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the catarrhal stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: ~1–2 weeks of coryzal symptoms indistinguishable from a cold (runny nose, mild cough, low-grade fever); the MOST infectious phase.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the paroxysmal stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: ~2–6 weeks of paroxysms — bursts of coughing ending in an inspiratory 'whoop' (forced inspiration against a closed glottis); post-tussive vomiting; worse at night; cyanosis/exhaustion. The whoop is often ABSENT in infants (→ apnoea instead) and in adults.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Describe the convalescent stage of pertussis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Weeks–months of gradual improvement; cough can linger for months, recurring with later URTIs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the classic clinical features of pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Coryzal prodrome → paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after a coughing fit); typically afebrile/low-grade; the child often looks WELL between fits.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What can coughing paroxysms in pertussis cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Cyanosis, subconjunctival haemorrhages, petechiae, syncope.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How does pertussis present in infants <6 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Atypically and dangerously — may have NO whoop; present with apnoea, cyanosis, poor feeding or a brief resolved unexplained event rather than the classic cough. This is the group to worry about.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is first-line investigation for pertussis in the early weeks?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: B. pertussis PCR (nasopharyngeal swab/aspirate) — most sensitive early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What investigation is used for pertussis in patients coughing >2 weeks?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Anti-pertussis toxin IgG serology / oral fluid testing — the mainstay of confirmation later, when PCR/culture sensitivity falls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What classic FBC finding occurs in pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Marked lymphocytosis (especially in infants).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: When should UKHSA be notified about pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: On clinical suspicion — don't wait for confirmation (it is a notifiable disease).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What do antibiotics achieve in pertussis, and when should they be given?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A macrolide if within 21 days of cough onset — they reduce infectivity/transmission but do little for symptoms once the paroxysmal (toxin-mediated) stage is established.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the antibiotic choice for pertussis by group?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: <1 month: clarithromycin. >1 month + non-pregnant adults: azithromycin or clarithromycin. Pregnant women: erythromycin. Macrolide-intolerant/contraindicated: co-trimoxazole (NOT in pregnancy or infants <6 weeks).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Who should be admitted with pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Infants — <6 months, apnoea/cyanosis, severe paroxysms, feeding difficulty, or complications (for oxygen, monitoring, feeding/fluid support, sometimes ICU).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the exclusion rules for pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Stay off school/nursery/work until 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics (or 21 days from cough onset if untreated).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Who receives chemoprophylaxis for pertussis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A macrolide for close contacts — targeted at vulnerable contacts (young infants, late-pregnancy women, and those in contact with them) per UKHSA guidance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the main complications of pertussis in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Apnoea, secondary pneumonia (commonest cause of death), pulmonary hypertension, seizures, encephalopathy (hypoxia) and death; and from the force of coughing: subconjunctival/nasal haemorrhage, rib fracture, hernia, syncope, pneumothorax.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: How is pertussis prevented by vaccination?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Routine childhood immunisation — pertussis is in the 6-in-1 vaccine (2, 3, 4 months) and the pre-school (4-in-1) booster; plus maternal vaccination in pregnancy (~16–32 weeks) — the key intervention to protect newborns via passive antibody transfer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why do older children and adults matter in pertussis epidemiology?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Immunity (vaccine or natural) wanes → they get milder disease and act as a reservoir for infants.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Recurrent wheezing in children under ~5 years, most commonly triggered by viral upper respiratory tract infections ('episodic viral wheeze').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why does preschool wheeze matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is extremely common (up to a third of preschoolers wheeze), a frequent cause of GP/ED attendance and admission, and the key challenges are distinguishing it from asthma (can't confidently diagnose asthma under 5) and managing acute episodes without over-treating.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the core concept behind preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Small preschool airways narrow easily when inflamed by a virus → wheeze during colds; most children grow out of it as their airways enlarge (usually by ~6), but ~1 in 3 who wheeze persistently develop asthma (especially with atopy/sensitisation and a family history).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is episodic viral wheeze (EVW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Wheeze ONLY with viral URTIs, symptom-free between episodes, with less underlying inflammation; often resolves by ~6.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Wheeze with viral URTIs PLUS other triggers (exercise, allergens, cold air, smoke), with interval symptoms (cough/wheeze between colds) and more underlying inflammation (closer to asthma); more likely to become asthma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the current caveat about the EVW/MTW distinction?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: It is less rigid than once taught — children move between phenotypes over time and parental reporting is imperfect; it is a useful framework but treatment is increasingly guided by frequency/severity and atopy risk rather than the label alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What features favour asthma / higher risk of progression in a preschool wheezer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Interval (between-episode) symptoms — cough/wheeze when well, night cough, exercise-induced wheeze; personal/family history of atopy (eczema, allergic rhinitis, food allergy, parental asthma — the Asthma Predictive Index); a clear response to a bronchodilator/ICS trial; frequent/severe exacerbations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Why do you generally NOT formally diagnose asthma under 5?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Can't do reliable spirometry and many will grow out of it — use a 'watch, treat, and review' approach and reassess with age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What are the typical clinical features of preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Wheeze + cough + increased work of breathing appearing WITH a viral cold (coryzal prodrome → wheeze); expiratory polyphonic wheeze, tachypnoea, recession; recurrent self-limiting episodes; well between episodes (EVW) or interval symptoms (MTW).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What red flags suggest an alternative diagnosis rather than simple preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Symptoms from birth/very early, failure to thrive, wet/productive chronic cough (CF, bronchiectasis), focal signs/stridor, choking episode (inhaled foreign body), finger clubbing, cardiac signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: Is preschool wheeze usually investigated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: No — it is a clinical diagnosis; consider CXR if atypical/red flags (exclude foreign body, structural/cardiac cause), sweat test if CF suspected. Spirometry is not reliable under ~5.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the mainstay of treating an acute preschool wheeze exacerbation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Inhaled SABA (salbutamol) via a spacer (± face mask), titrated to response (burst therapy then spacing out); oxygen if hypoxic; oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) for moderate–severe exacerbations; escalate as for acute asthma if severe.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: When should a child with acute preschool wheeze be admitted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: If poor response, hypoxia, severe distress, or unable to feed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the preventer approach for episodic viral wheeze (EVW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: First-line: SABA (or anticholinergic/ipratropium) via spacer as needed for episodes. Second-line (if frequent/severe): intermittent LTRA (montelukast) and/or intermittent ICS started at the onset of a viral episode.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What is the preventer approach for multiple-trigger wheeze (MTW)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: A trial of a regular preventer — ICS or LTRA (montelukast) — for 4–8 weeks, then REVIEW; continue only if clear benefit (a treatment trial, not open-ended). ICS tends to work better in MTW than EVW.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What general measures are advised in preschool wheeze?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Avoid tobacco smoke exposure (a major modifiable trigger), inhaler technique/spacer education, and a written action plan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.front: What safety counselling is needed for montelukast?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Lower Respirato.back: Counsel about neuropsychiatric side effects — sleep disturbance, mood/behaviour change, nightmares (a recent safety emphasis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What conditions are grouped under neonatal GI & abdominal wall?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Congenital gut and abdominal-wall anomalies plus the acquired bowel emergency of prematurity (NEC).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the organising principle for neonatal GI & abdominal wall conditions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Many present with neonatal bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, failure to pass meconium) or are seen at birth (abdominal-wall defects); NEC is an acquired emergency in preterm/formula-fed neonates.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue for duodenal atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Bilious vomiting, 'double bubble' on X-ray; associated with Down syndrome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue and management for biliary atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Prolonged conjugated jaundice, pale stools/dark urine; Kasai portoenterostomy early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do gastroschisis and omphalocele differ at a glance?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis (no sac, right of cord, isolated) vs omphalocele (sac, associated anomalies).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Give the clue and management for necrotising enterocolitis (NEC).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Preterm; feeding intolerance, distension, bloody stool, pneumatosis → stop feeds, antibiotics, surgery if perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does prolonged conjugated jaundice with pale stools mean until proven otherwise?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia → urgent referral (Kasai success depends on early surgery).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A congenital complete obstruction of the duodenal lumen — the commonest cause of congenital (proximal) small-bowel obstruction in the neonate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the core mechanism of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Failure of recanalisation of the duodenal lumen during the ~8th week of fetal development (the duodenum normally becomes a solid cord then re-hollows; if it doesn't → an atretic blind-ending segment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does duodenal atresia's mechanism differ from distal (jejunal/ileal) atresias?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Duodenal atresia is failure of recanalisation, whereas distal atresias have an ischaemic/vascular cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is most duodenal atresia vomiting bilious?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Because ~85% of obstructions are distal to the ampulla of Vater, so bile enters above the obstruction (green vomit); a proximal one (~15%) is non-bilious.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key rule about any bilious vomiting in a neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is a surgical emergency until obstruction is excluded — the key differential being malrotation with volvulus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: When does duodenal atresia present and how?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Vomiting within the first day of life (complete obstruction presents early); usually bilious (distal to ampulla), non-bilious if proximal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the abdomen typically like in duodenal atresia, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Often scaphoid/flat distally with only epigastric (or no) distension — the obstruction is high so distal bowel is empty/gasless, unlike distal obstructions which distend the whole abdomen. Failure to pass meconium may occur; excessive salivation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How may duodenal atresia be picked up antenatally?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Polyhydramnios (fetus can't swallow/absorb amniotic fluid past the obstruction) plus a double bubble on the fetal ultrasound.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the classic association of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — ~1/3 of cases; karyotyping is indicated.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: List other associations of duodenal atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Congenital heart disease (~half); annular pancreas, malrotation, oesophageal atresia/TOF, imperforate anus, renal anomalies, biliary anomalies (VACTERL-type); prematurity, maternal polyhydramnios.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the 'double bubble' sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Two gas-filled bubbles (dilated stomach + dilated proximal duodenum) with no/little gas distally on abdominal X-ray — usually diagnostic of duodenal atresia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does gas distal to the double bubble suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Duodenal stenosis (partial) or, importantly, malrotation/volvulus rather than complete atresia — a crucial distinction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What investigations are done for the associations of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Echocardiography and karyotype (screen the associations); electrolytes for dehydration/losses; upper GI contrast study + ultrasound for equivocal cases/to exclude malrotation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the immediate/supportive management of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Nasogastric tube (decompress the stomach), IV fluid resuscitation, and correct electrolyte disturbance (vomiting → hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis) — stabilise first.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the definitive treatment of duodenal atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Surgical repair — duodenoduodenostomy (bypass the atretic segment, joining the two duodenal ends); good outcomes. Screen/manage associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A progressive, obliterative cholangiopathy of the newborn — inflammatory destruction and fibrosis of the bile ducts blocking bile flow (obstructive cholestasis); if untreated leads to cirrhosis, liver failure and death by ~2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why does biliary atresia matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is the commonest surgical cause of neonatal cholestasis and the leading indication for paediatric liver transplantation; outcome depends entirely on early diagnosis and surgery (Kasai works far better before ~60 days).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe the core mechanism of biliary atresia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Progressive inflammation and fibrosis obliterate the extrahepatic (± intrahepatic) bile ducts → bile can't drain → conjugated (direct) bilirubin backs up → progressive hepatic fibrosis → cirrhosis. Cause unknown (likely immune/inflammatory ± viral/genetic).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What causes of jaundice does a conjugated (direct) picture suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia, neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, infection, metabolic (galactosaemia, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency) — pathological, needs urgent work-up.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What causes of jaundice does an unconjugated (indirect) picture suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Physiological jaundice, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis — usually benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the stool and urine findings in biliary atresia (obstructive) vs benign unconjugated jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary atresia: pale stools + dark urine (obstructive). Benign unconjugated: normal-coloured stools/urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is THE rule for prolonged neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Any term infant still jaundiced at >14 days (or preterm >21 days) → do a jaundice screen including a SPLIT bilirubin; a raised conjugated fraction → think biliary atresia until proven otherwise.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the presenting feature of biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Persistent (prolonged) neonatal jaundice beyond 2 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why can pale/acholic stools be a missed clue in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Pale clay-coloured stools mean no bile pigment reaches the gut, but they can be overlooked → false reassurance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is urine dark in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble → excreted renally, darkening the urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is the early presentation of biliary atresia a trap?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: The baby often initially looks well and thrives early on; hepatomegaly develops, and only later (if untreated, >3 months) come hepatosplenomegaly, faltering growth, ascites, coagulopathy (vitamin K malabsorption) and cirrhosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is BASM syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Biliary Atresia Splenic Malformation syndrome (~10–15%) — polysplenia/asplenia, situs inversus, cardiac defects, intestinal malrotation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key first test in suspected biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A SPLIT (conjugated/unconjugated) bilirubin — showing a raised conjugated (direct) fraction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What LFT findings occur in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Raised transaminases and especially raised GGT; plus a coagulation screen (vitamin-K-dependent factors; bleeding risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What does the jaundice screen include for biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: TFTs (hypothyroid), FBC/blood film, urine MC&S (UTI), U&E, galactosaemia screen, infection/TORCH, alpha-1-antitrypsin, metabolic tests.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What ultrasound findings suggest biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Absent/abnormal gallbladder and the 'triangular cord' sign; ultrasound also excludes a choledochal cyst.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What do HIDA scan and liver biopsy show in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: HIDA (hepatobiliary) scan — no excretion of tracer into the bowel. Liver biopsy — bile duct proliferation, fibrosis. Intra-operative cholangiogram is the definitive/confirmatory test.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the first-line surgical treatment of biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Kasai portoenterostomy — a Roux loop of jejunum anastomosed to the porta hepatis to allow bile drainage, bypassing the obliterated extrahepatic ducts.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why is the timing of the Kasai procedure critical?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Best outcomes if done before ~60 days of life (some say <45 days); the older the infant, the worse the result — age at surgery is the single most important prognostic factor.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What supportive management is needed in biliary atresia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K), nutritional support (MCT-based feeds), ursodeoxycholic acid, and treating/preventing cholangitis (a common post-Kasai complication).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the definitive treatment if Kasai fails or cirrhosis develops?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Liver transplantation — biliary atresia is the commonest indication for paediatric liver transplant; many children ultimately need one even after a successful Kasai.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: The two congenital anterior abdominal wall defects in which abdominal contents herniate out through the wall at birth; usually diagnosed antenatally.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What single feature separates gastroschisis from omphalocele and drives everything?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: The presence of a covering sac: gastroschisis has NO sac (bowel exposed); omphalocele has a sac (amnion + peritoneum).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Where is the defect in gastroschisis vs omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis: lateral to the cord (usually to the right). Omphalocele: at/through the umbilicus itself.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do the associations differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis: few/none (usually isolated). Omphalocele: strong chromosomal and syndromic associations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What happens to the bowel in gastroschisis vs omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis: exposed → inflamed, matted, at risk of ischaemia/atresia. Omphalocele: protected by the sac (unless it ruptures).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does the delivery plan differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis: vaginal delivery can be attempted. Omphalocele: C-section (protect the sac from rupture).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How does the repair differ between gastroschisis and omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis: urgent — theatre ASAP (± silo). Omphalocele: staged/gradual closure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe gastroschisis in detail.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A full-thickness defect lateral to the cord (usually right) with NO covering sac → bowel exposed to amniotic fluid → inflamed, thickened, matted ('peel'), at risk of ischaemia, atresia and heat/fluid loss.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the risk factors for gastroschisis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Young maternal age (<20), maternal smoking, alcohol and recreational drug use; incidence is rising. Usually isolated with few associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How is gastroschisis managed after birth?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Newborn to theatre ASAP — primary closure if possible, or a 'silo' (bowel suspended and gradually reduced over days before closure).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe omphalocele (exomphalos).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Protrusion of abdominal contents through the abdominal wall at the umbilicus, covered by a sac of amniotic membrane and peritoneum; may contain bowel, liver and other viscera.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What chromosomal associations does omphalocele have?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Trisomy 13 (Patau), 18 (Edwards), 21 (Down) → karyotyping is essential.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and its link to omphalocele?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Exomphalos + macroglossia + gigantism/overgrowth + neonatal hypoglycaemia (+ Wilms'/hepatoblastoma risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What other associations does omphalocele have?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Cardiac defects (common — echo needed), Pentalogy of Cantrell, cloacal exstrophy, renal anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How is omphalocele managed (delivery and repair)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: C-section to reduce risk of sac rupture; staged repair — gradual closure over 6–12 months so the abdominal cavity/pulmonary system can accommodate returning contents (forcing a large volume back suddenly → respiratory compromise/abdominal compartment syndrome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How are both abdominal wall defects usually diagnosed antenatally, and what marker is raised?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Both are usually detected on the routine 20-week ultrasound; maternal serum AFP is raised in both (higher in gastroschisis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What antenatal investigations does omphalocele need vs gastroschisis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Omphalocele → karyotyping (amniocentesis) + echocardiography + renal ultrasound (screen associations). Gastroschisis → fewer investigations (usually isolated), serial growth scans (IUGR risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the immediate neonatal management of an abdominal wall defect?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Cover the exposed bowel/defect (clingfilm/clear occlusive covering or 'bowel bag'), fluid resuscitation (large insensible losses), thermoregulation, nasogastric tube (decompress bowel), IV antibiotics; monitor bowel perfusion, then surgical closure (primary or staged/silo).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: How do the prognoses of gastroschisis and omphalocele compare?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Gastroschisis is generally good (isolated); omphalocele prognosis depends on associated anomalies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is necrotising enterocolitis (NEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: A devastating inflammatory bowel disease of the neonate — inflammation, ischaemia and bacterial invasion of the bowel wall → necrosis, which can progress to perforation, peritonitis and death.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Why does NEC matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: It is the commonest GI emergency in the neonatal unit and one of the leading causes of death in premature infants; strongly linked to prematurity and enteral (especially formula) feeding, with breast milk protective. Survivors risk short bowel syndrome, strictures and neurodevelopmental impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: Describe the core mechanism ('perfect storm') of NEC.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Immature intestinal barrier + abnormal bacterial colonisation (dysbiosis) + mucosal ischaemia/hypoperfusion + enteral feed as substrate → bacteria breach the fragile bowel wall → inflammation and ischaemic necrosis → gas tracks into the bowel wall (pneumatosis) and portal system → perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: When does NEC typically cluster?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: In preterm, formula-fed babies after feeds are established (typically weeks 2–4).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the biggest risk factors for NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Prematurity + very low birth weight (the more preterm, the higher the risk); formula feeding (breast milk is protective).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: List other risk factors for NEC.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: IUGR/placental insufficiency, hypoxia/perinatal asphyxia; anything reducing gut perfusion — congenital heart disease (especially duct-dependent/PDA), polycythaemia, exchange/RBC transfusion, sepsis, hypotension; rapid advancement of enteral feeds.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the early clinical features of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Feeding intolerance (increased/bilious gastric aspirates, vomiting often bile-stained), abdominal distension (often the first sign, ± tenderness/visible loops), and bloody stools (blood/mucus per rectum).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the systemic and late/severe features of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Systemic: lethargy, temperature instability, apnoea/bradycardia, poor perfusion → sepsis/shock, DIC. Severe/late: abdominal wall discolouration (erythema), perforation, peritonitis — needing surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the key investigation in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Abdominal X-ray.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What abdominal X-ray findings occur in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Dilated bowel loops; bowel wall oedema (thickened wall); pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas — the pathognomonic sign); portal venous gas (more severe); pneumoperitoneum → perforation (Rigler's sign — gas both sides of the bowel wall; 'football sign').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the pathognomonic X-ray sign of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Pneumatosis intestinalis — gas within the bowel wall.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What blood findings occur in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Thrombocytopenia (a useful early clue), anaemia, leukocytosis/leukopenia; metabolic acidosis; raised CRP; blood culture (sepsis); coagulation/DIC screen; blood gas.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is Bell staging used for in NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Staging NEC I (suspected) → II (definite) → III (advanced/perforation) on clinical + radiological features, guiding management.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the medical (Bell I–II) management of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Stop enteral feeds (bowel rest/nil by mouth) and NG tube on free drainage (decompress); typically bowel rest ~7–14 days with parenteral nutrition; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (Gram-negatives and anaerobes); supportive care (IV fluids, correct acidosis/electrolytes, respiratory/circulatory support, treat DIC/thrombocytopenia); serial X-rays and examinations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the surgical (Bell III) management of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: For perforation or deterioration despite medical management: laparotomy with resection of necrotic bowel (± stoma); peritoneal drain in the very small/unstable. Pneumoperitoneum is an indication for surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What are the complications of NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Perforation/peritonitis, sepsis/DIC, strictures (later), short bowel syndrome (after resection → long-term parenteral nutrition), neurodevelopmental impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What is the single most important protective factor against NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Breast milk (maternal or donor).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.front: What other measures help prevent NEC?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal GI & A.back: Antenatal corticosteroids (if preterm delivery anticipated — gut maturation), cautious/standardised feeding protocols, and probiotics (increasingly used to reduce NEC in preterms).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the organising principle for neonatal medicine problems?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Prematurity and perinatal events drive most neonatal illness; approach by system — breathing (RDS, meconium aspiration), metabolic (jaundice, hypoglycaemia), infection (sepsis) and brain (HIE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Preterm surfactant deficiency; grunting, ground-glass X-ray; antenatal steroids, surfactant, CPAP.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for meconium aspiration syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Term/post-term, meconium-stained liquor; respiratory distress; supportive/ventilation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key rule for neonatal jaundice.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: <24h = always pathological (haemolysis/sepsis); phototherapy/exchange by threshold; kernicterus risk.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal sepsis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Non-specific (temperature instability, poor feeding); cultures + empirical antibiotics promptly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Perinatal hypoxia; encephalopathy; therapeutic cooling within 6h.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Give the key points for neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Jittery, poor feeding, seizures; at-risk (IUGR, IDM, preterm); feed / IV dextrose.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: An acute lung disease of the newborn caused by insufficient pulmonary surfactant → alveolar collapse and stiff, poorly-inflated lungs (also called surfactant deficient lung disease / hyaline membrane disease).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does RDS matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in premature infants, its incidence rises the more preterm the baby, and antenatal corticosteroids and exogenous surfactant have transformed survival.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core mechanism of RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes (mature ~weeks 24–34). In prematurity, insufficient surfactant + structural lung immaturity → high alveolar surface tension → alveolar collapse (atelectasis) → stiff/non-compliant lungs; blood passing collapsed alveoli isn't oxygenated (intrapulmonary shunt) → hypoxaemia + increased work of breathing.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is surfactant's job?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: To lower surface tension and stop alveoli collapsing — so its absence is the whole disease of RDS.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the biggest risk factor for RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Prematurity — risk is inversely proportional to gestational age (very common <28 weeks, uncommon at term).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List other risk factors for RDS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Male sex; maternal diabetes (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant production); caesarean section (especially without labour); second twin, perinatal asphyxia/hypothermia, family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When does RDS present and how does it evolve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Onset within minutes–hours of birth (typically <4 hours), worsening over the first ~48–72 h.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the clinical signs of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Tachypnoea, intercostal (± subcostal) recession, expiratory grunting (auto-PEEP against a closed glottis), cyanosis, nasal flaring, apnoea in the very preterm.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the chest X-ray appearance of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: 'Ground-glass' appearance — diffuse fine reticulogranular shadowing + air bronchograms + reduced lung volumes, with an indistinct heart border (from widespread atelectasis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What blood gas findings occur in RDS, and what must be excluded?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, respiratory ± metabolic acidosis. Screen for/exclude sepsis (congenital pneumonia e.g. Group B Strep can look identical).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the antenatal prevention of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Maternal (antenatal) corticosteroids to induce fetal lung maturation — given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (e.g. <34–36 weeks); reduces RDS, IVH and neonatal death.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the first-line postnatal respiratory support for RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: CPAP — keeps alveoli open and often avoids intubation, escalating to mechanical ventilation if needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is exogenous surfactant given in RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Via an endotracheal tube — replacing the missing surfactant; increasingly given by minimally invasive techniques (LISA/MIST — a thin catheter without full intubation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive care is needed in RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Thermoregulation, fluids/nutrition, treat sepsis, gentle handling.
