conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the complications of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Pneumothorax/air leak (stiff lungs + positive-pressure ventilation); bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen need beyond 36 weeks corrected age); IVH, patent ductus arteriosus, retinopathy of prematurity, NEC, infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Chronic lung disease of prematurity — an oxygen requirement persisting beyond 36 weeks corrected age (from lung injury + oxygen/ventilation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the key differentials of RDS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN — term/C-section, self-resolves ~24–48h) and congenital pneumonia (Group B Strep).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Respiratory distress in a newborn caused by aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid (MSAF) into the lungs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does MAS matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is an important cause of respiratory distress in TERM and POST-TERM infants (opposite end of the spectrum to RDS), causes disease through multiple mechanisms at once, and is strongly linked to persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core sequence leading to MAS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal distress/hypoxia (or maturity) → the fetus passes meconium into the amniotic fluid AND gasps → meconium is inhaled into the airways.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the four ways meconium causes disease in the lungs?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: (1) Airway obstruction — 'ball-valve' → air trapping/hyperinflation (pneumothorax) and atelectasis; (2) chemical pneumonitis/inflammation; (3) surfactant inactivation (free fatty/bile acids); (4) persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is PPHN in the context of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Hypoxia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → the circulation reverts to a right-to-left (fetal-type) shunt → refractory hypoxaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the single most important risk factor for MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal distress / intrapartum hypoxia-asphyxia (hypoxia → meconium passage + gasping).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List other risk factors for MAS.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Post-term/post-maturity (mature gut passes meconium more readily), small-for-gestational-age/IUGR, placental insufficiency, difficult/prolonged labour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What does meconium-stained liquor in preterm labour suggest?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is rare in preterm labour — if present, think chorioamnionitis/infection or cord compression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the clinical features of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Onset immediately/soon after birth in a term/post-term baby; meconium-stained (green) liquor and staining of skin/nails/cord; respiratory distress (tachypnoea, grunting, flaring, recession, cyanosis); often a barrel/hyperinflated chest; crackles/rhonchi; may be depressed/asphyxiated at birth (low Apgars). Watch for PPHN — severe/labile hypoxaemia out of proportion to lung findings.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the chest X-ray appearance of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Patchy infiltrates and atelectasis, with hyperinflation and areas of consolidation/collapse; ± pneumothorax/air leak.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What investigations are used if PPHN is suspected in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Pre-/post-ductal saturations + echocardiography (right-to-left shunt); plus blood gas and a sepsis screen (MAS mimics/co-exists with congenital pneumonia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the current delivery-room approach to meconium-stained babies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Routine deep endotracheal suctioning is NO LONGER recommended — even non-vigorous infants: follow normal neonatal resuscitation (airway, breathing). Suction only if the airway is obstructed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the mainstay of postnatal management of MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Supportive — oxygen and respiratory support (CPAP/mechanical ventilation as needed; HFOV in severe cases); careful because air trapping + atelectasis make ventilation tricky.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the role of surfactant in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Exogenous surfactant and/or surfactant lavage in moderate–severe MAS, because meconium inactivates surfactant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is PPHN treated in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) — a pulmonary vasodilator; ECMO as rescue in refractory PPHN/respiratory failure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What additional supportive measures are used in MAS?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Antibiotics (can't exclude infection), thermoregulation, fluids, treat air leaks (chest drain for pneumothorax), monitor for hypoxic-ischaemic injury.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Yellow discolouration of the skin/sclera from raised bilirubin (hyperbilirubinaemia) in a newborn; extremely common (>50% of term, most preterm babies) — usually benign/physiological, but a minority is pathological and dangerous.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal jaundice matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cross the blood-brain barrier and cause kernicterus (permanent brain injury); the clinical skill is using the TIMING to separate benign from serious.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why are newborns predisposed to jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: High red-cell mass with a short lifespan (rapid breakdown of fetal Hb → more bilirubin) + an immature liver (low UGT enzyme activity → can't conjugate fast enough) + increased enterohepatic circulation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at <24 hours interpreted, and what are the causes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: ALWAYS pathological — usually haemolysis: Rhesus & ABO haemolytic disease, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency; plus congenital infection/sepsis (TORCH). Check serum bilirubin urgently (within ~2 hours).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at day 2–14 usually interpreted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Usually physiological (or breastfeeding/breast-milk jaundice) — unconjugated, benign; peaks day 3–5, resolves by ~day 10–14, baby is well and feeding. A diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is jaundice at >14 days (>21 days if preterm) interpreted?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Prolonged — pathological until proven otherwise → jaundice screen. Causes: biliary atresia, hypothyroidism, galactosaemia, UTI, breast-milk jaundice, prematurity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the difference between breastfeeding jaundice and breast-milk jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Breastfeeding jaundice — early, from suboptimal intake/dehydration → more enterohepatic circulation. Breast-milk jaundice — later/prolonged, benign, from breast-milk factors (a common cause of prolonged jaundice in a thriving baby).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How does prematurity affect physiological jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It exaggerates and prolongs it (immature liver + shorter red-cell survival).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What does a jaundice screen include for prolonged jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Conjugated + unconjugated (split) bilirubin, Coombs (DAT), TFTs, FBC (± film), urine MC&S, U&E, LFTs (+ blood group, G6PD, infection/metabolic screen).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why is the split bilirubin the key branch point in prolonged jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Conjugated (>~25 µmol/L or >20%) → pathological → biliary atresia until proven otherwise (pale stools/dark urine), neonatal hepatitis, choledochal cyst, metabolic. Unconjugated → hypothyroidism, UTI/infection, breast-milk jaundice, haemolysis, galactosaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is bilirubin measured in a jaundiced newborn?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transcutaneous bilirubinometer (screening, ≥35 weeks & >24h) → serum bilirubin (SBR) to confirm/if high-risk; always SBR if <24 hours old or <35 weeks.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What decides treatment in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Plotting the SBR against age (hours) on the gestational-age-specific NICE treatment threshold chart, comparing the level to the phototherapy and exchange lines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is first-line treatment for neonatal jaundice, and how does it work?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Phototherapy — blue light (~450 nm) converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin to water-soluble isomers excreted without conjugation. Escalate to multiple/intensified phototherapy if rising fast or nearing the exchange threshold.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When is IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) used in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: As an adjunct in Rhesus/ABO haemolytic disease when bilirubin keeps rising despite intensive phototherapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: When is exchange transfusion used in neonatal jaundice?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: For very high/rapidly rising bilirubin (above the exchange line, or signs of bilirubin encephalopathy) — removes bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells; prevents kernicterus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Which type of bilirubin causes kernicterus and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Only UNCONJUGATED (fat-soluble) bilirubin — it crosses the blood-brain barrier; conjugated is water-soluble and doesn't. This is why the split matters and why unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is treated aggressively.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia → then irritability, hypertonia, arching (opisthotonos), high-pitched cry, seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the chronic (permanent) sequelae of kernicterus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upward-gaze palsy, dental enamel dysplasia, learning difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: A systemic bacterial infection in the first 28 days of life — a medical emergency; newborns have an immature immune system, deteriorate rapidly, and present with vague, non-specific signs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal sepsis matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is a major cause of neonatal death and disability; Group B Streptococcus and E. coli are the leading organisms; the approach is 'treat first, ask questions later' — take cultures and start antibiotics within 1 hour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is early-onset vs late-onset neonatal sepsis defined by timing?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Early-onset: <72 hours (often <24 h) of life. Late-onset: >72 hours to 28 days.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the sources and organisms of early-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Source: vertical — from the mother (birth canal/ascending infection). Organisms: Group B Strep + E. coli (also Listeria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the sources and organisms of late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Source: environmental/nosocomial (hands, lines, ventilators). Organisms: coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (esp. lines), Staph aureus, Gram-negatives, Group B Strep, fungal (Candida).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List the maternal/early-onset risk factors for neonatal sepsis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Maternal Group B Strep (colonisation, GBS bacteriuria, or a previous baby with invasive GBS disease); prolonged rupture of membranes (>18–24 h); preterm labour/prematurity; chorioamnionitis/maternal intrapartum fever (>38°C) or confirmed maternal infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the risk factors for late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Preterm, low birth weight, indwelling lines/devices, prolonged neonatal-unit stay.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the non-specific clinical features of neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Respiratory (grunting, tachypnoea, apnoea, increased O2 need, cyanosis), temperature instability (fever OR — more commonly — hypothermia), poor feeding/vomiting/distension, lethargy/irritability/hypotonia/seizures/bulging fontanelle, poor perfusion/mottling/hypotension, jaundice (especially <24 h), hypo-/hyperglycaemia, metabolic acidosis, DIC/bleeding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the NICE 'red flag' signs of neonatal sepsis prompting immediate treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Signs of shock, seizures, need for mechanical ventilation, respiratory distress starting >4 h after birth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the key investigation in neonatal sepsis, and when is it taken?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Blood culture — BEFORE the first antibiotic dose (but don't delay antibiotics for it).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What other investigations are used in neonatal sepsis (NICE NG195)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: FBC (neutropenia/neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia), CRP (baseline and repeated ~18–24 h to trend); lumbar puncture if strong suspicion/meningitis signs/culture-positive; blood gas, glucose, U&E; surface/urine cultures, CXR as indicated; late-onset → sample lines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the empirical antibiotic regimen for early-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Benzylpenicillin + gentamicin (the standard UK regimen — covers Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the empirical antibiotic regimen for late-onset sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Flucloxacillin + gentamicin (or per local policy — cover coagulase-negative staph/line infection; add Gram-negative/Listeria cover as needed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How quickly must antibiotics be started in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Within 1 hour of deciding to treat — don't wait for results (NICE NG195).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive care is needed in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Respiratory support (O2/ventilation), fluids/inotropes for shock, glucose, correct acidosis/coagulopathy (DIC), thermoregulation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How are antibiotics reviewed in neonatal sepsis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: At ~36 hours: stop if the baby is well, blood cultures are negative and CRP is normal/falling; continue (≥7 days, longer for meningitis) if culture-positive or ongoing suspicion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is early-onset Group B Strep sepsis prevented?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) — IV benzylpenicillin in labour for at-risk mothers (GBS colonisation/bacteriuria, previous GBS baby, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrapartum fever).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Neonatal brain injury caused by insufficient oxygen and blood flow to the brain (perinatal asphyxia), usually around the time of birth.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does HIE matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: It is a major cause of neonatal death and long-term neurodisability (cerebral palsy, epilepsy, cognitive/sensory impairment), and therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) started within 6 hours is the one intervention proven to reduce death and disability.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the 'two-phase' injury of HIE and why the 6-hour window exists.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Primary energy failure during the insult (cells can't make ATP → ion pumps fail → cell death) → a latent phase (~6 hours) as circulation is restored (the therapeutic window) → secondary energy failure (~6–48 h) of excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis causing delayed neuronal death. Cooling slows this secondary cascade, so it must start within ~6 hours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List causes of HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Placental abruption, cord prolapse/compression, uterine rupture, shoulder dystocia, maternal hypotension/shock, prolonged/obstructed labour, failure to breathe at birth, severe anaemia (feto-maternal haemorrhage), maternal hypoxia, meconium aspiration.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What evidence of perinatal asphyxia supports HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Low Apgar scores (≤5 at 10 min), need for prolonged resuscitation, and metabolic acidosis (cord pH <7.0 or base deficit ≥16).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the features of encephalopathy in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Altered consciousness (irritability → lethargy → coma), abnormal tone (hypo-/hypertonia), poor feeding/weak suck, abnormal/primitive reflexes, seizures, apnoea, abnormal posturing/movements.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What multi-organ involvement supports HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction (deranged LFTs), cardiac dysfunction, DIC (hypoxia hits other organs too).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 1 (mild) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Irritable/hyperalert consciousness, normal/slightly increased tone, exaggerated startle, no seizures; usually good prognosis (recovers ~24–48 h); no cooling.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 2 (moderate) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Lethargic consciousness, hypotonia, weak suck, seizures common; variable prognosis (~1/3 have long-term problems); cool.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe modified Sarnat grade 3 (severe) HIE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Comatose, flaccid tone, absent suck/reflexes, frequent/prolonged seizures; poor prognosis (high death/severe disability); cool.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Which Sarnat grades receive therapeutic cooling?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Grades 2–3 (moderate–severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What investigations are used in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Cord/arterial blood gas (acidosis), glucose, U&E, LFTs, FBC, coagulation (multi-organ screen); aEEG/EEG (background activity + detect often-subclinical seizures, prognostic); MRI brain (usually days 5–14, defines injury pattern, prognostic); cranial ultrasound.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the key intervention in HIE and its parameters?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) — cool to ~33–34°C for 72 hours, started within 6 hours of birth, for moderate–severe (Sarnat 2–3) HIE in infants ≥36 weeks; reduces death and disability (TOBY/NICHD trials); then rewarm slowly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What supportive intensive care is needed alongside cooling in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Ventilation as needed (maintain normal oxygenation/CO2); treat seizures (phenobarbital first-line); maintain normoglycaemia, normal BP/perfusion, fluid/electrolyte balance; treat multi-organ dysfunction; avoid hyperthermia (worsens injury); monitor for infection.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the first-line treatment for seizures in HIE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Phenobarbital.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What determines prognosis in HIE, and what are the sequelae?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Severity (Sarnat grade): grade 1 usually normal, grade 2 variable, grade 3 high mortality/severe disability. Sequelae: cerebral palsy (especially dyskinetic/spastic quadriplegic), epilepsy, learning disability, sensorineural hearing loss, visual impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: A low blood glucose in the newborn — the commonest metabolic problem in neonates.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why does neonatal hypoglycaemia matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Transient mild hypoglycaemia in the first hours is common and usually benign (transition from constant placental glucose to intermittent feeds), but persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia can cause permanent brain injury (the brain depends on glucose).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Describe the core physiology of neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: At birth the placental glucose supply is suddenly cut off → the newborn must mobilise its own glucose (glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis) and establish feeding. A transient dip is normal; problems arise when demand outstrips supply, stores are low, or consumption is high.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why do infants of diabetic mothers get hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia (from maternal hyperglycaemia) persists after birth → the baby keeps over-secreting insulin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: List the at-risk groups for persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Infant of a diabetic mother (fetal hyperinsulinaemia), prematurity (low glycogen stores), IUGR/SGA (low stores), large-for-dates, hypothermia (increased consumption), neonatal sepsis, perinatal asphyxia/stress, polycythaemia, inborn errors of metabolism, congenital hyperinsulinism (nesidioblastosis), Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, endocrine deficiency (hypopituitarism, cortisol/growth hormone deficiency).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the autonomic features of neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Jitteriness (the classic sign), irritability, tachypnoea, pallor, sweating.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What are the neuroglycopenic features of neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Poor feeding/sucking, weak/high-pitched cry, drowsiness/lethargy, hypotonia, seizures, apnoea, coma (severe).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: Why must at-risk babies be screened for hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Because hypoglycaemia may be asymptomatic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is blood glucose measured/confirmed in neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Screen at-risk infants with pre-feed capillary glucose; confirm low readings with a laboratory glucose (bedside glucometers are unreliable at low values).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is the operational treatment threshold for neonatal hypoglycaemia?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Treat/act at <2.6 mmol/L in at-risk/symptomatic babies (commonly used UK/BAPM threshold); symptomatic or very low → urgent action.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: What is a hypoglycaemia screen and when is it taken?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Taken WHEN glucose is low, for persistent/severe hypoglycaemia: insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids, lactate, ammonia, and metabolic/acylcarnitine studies — to identify hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency or an inborn error of metabolism.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is asymptomatic/mildly low neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Encourage normal/early feeding and monitor blood glucose — frequent feeds (breast/formula), keep warm, recheck pre-feeds; add buccal (40%) dextrose gel massaged into the cheek alongside feeding (reduces neonatal-unit admissions, supports breastfeeding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is symptomatic or very low neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Admit to the neonatal unit + IV 10% dextrose — glucose infusion (bolus then maintenance); escalate concentration/rate as needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.front: How is refractory/persistent neonatal hypoglycaemia managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neonatal Medici.back: Investigate the cause (hypoglycaemia screen); hyperinsulinism → diazoxide (± octreotide); treat endocrine deficiency; specialist metabolic/endocrine input. Aim to maintain glucose in a safe range and avoid recurrent/prolonged hypoglycaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the triad of nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema — caused by increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier to protein.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why does paediatric nephrotic syndrome matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: It is the commonest glomerular disorder of childhood; unlike adults it is overwhelmingly minimal change disease (~90%), which is steroid-responsive, so children are treated empirically with steroids WITHOUT a biopsy; and its complications (infection, thrombosis) can be life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Describe the core mechanism of nephrotic syndrome (minimal change).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Podocyte foot-process effacement makes the glomerular barrier leaky → massive protein (mainly albumin) leaks into urine → proteinuria → hypoalbuminaemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts into tissues → oedema. (In minimal change the glomeruli look 'normal' on light microscopy — effacement is seen only on electron microscopy.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How is nephrotic-range proteinuria defined in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Heavy proteinuria — >40 mg/m²/hour or a very high urine protein:creatinine ratio (adult equivalent >3.5 g/day); 'frothy urine'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What albumin level defines hypoalbuminaemia in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Serum albumin <25 g/L (albumin lost in urine).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Describe the oedema of nephrotic syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Periorbital classically (puffy eyes in the morning), then peripheral, ascites, scrotal/labial, ± anasarca.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the common fourth feature of nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Hyperlipidaemia — the liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to low albumin.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the dominant cause of nephrotic syndrome in children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Minimal change disease (~90%) — steroid-responsive, often following a viral URTI (contrast adults, where membranous is common).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is FSGS and how does it behave?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — more often steroid-resistant; commoner in older children/certain ethnicities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Name secondary causes of nephrotic syndrome to consider if atypical.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Henoch-Schönlein purpura, SLE (lupus nephritis), infection (HIV, hepatitis), diabetes; also membranoproliferative and (rarely in kids) membranous GN.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is congenital nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Nephrotic syndrome presenting <3 months (e.g. NPHS1/nephrin mutations) — severe and not steroid-responsive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is the classic age and sex distribution of minimal change nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Age 2–5 years; boys > girls.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is often the first sign of nephrotic syndrome, and what is it mistaken for?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Periorbital puffiness — often mistaken for allergy — then generalised oedema (ascites, peripheral, scrotal) and frothy urine.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What are the typical renal findings in minimal change disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Usually normotensive with normal renal function; weight gain and reduced urine output. Features suggesting otherwise are atypical → biopsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What atypical features suggest NOT minimal change disease and warrant biopsy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Hypertension, haematuria, impaired renal function, age <1 or >12 years, or steroid resistance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What urine investigations are used in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Urine dipstick + urine protein:creatinine ratio (uPCR) — heavy proteinuria (3+/4+; nephrotic-range uPCR).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What blood/other investigations are done in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Serum albumin (low <25), U&E/creatinine, FBC, lipids; look for cause/complications — complement (C3/C4), ASO/anti-DNase, ANA/anti-dsDNA, hepatitis/HIV, ± varicella immunity before steroids.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: When is renal biopsy indicated in childhood nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: NOT routine in typical cases — reserved for atypical features or steroid resistance (the empirical steroid trial IS the 'test' in typical minimal change).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What is first-line treatment for typical childhood nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Oral prednisolone — WITHOUT a biopsy: high-dose (e.g. ~60 mg/m²/day) then tapering; ~80–90% of minimal change disease responds ('steroid-sensitive').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: What supportive management is used in nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Salt and fluid restriction; diuretics (careful — intravascular depletion) for severe oedema; IV albumin for severe symptomatic oedema/hypovolaemia; penicillin prophylaxis; treat/prevent complications.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How are steroid-resistant/frequent-relapsing/steroid-dependent cases managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Biopsy + second-line agents — calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus/ciclosporin), levamisole, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab; ACE inhibitors (reduce proteinuria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How is paediatric nephrotic syndrome classified (not by biopsy)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: By steroid response: steroid-sensitive (remission with steroids, ~90%, usually minimal change); steroid-resistant (no remission after ~4 weeks → biopsy, often FSGS); and relapsing/frequently-relapsing/steroid-dependent (relapses on tapering/stopping).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why do children with nephrotic syndrome get infections, and how is this managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Loss of immunoglobulins + complement in urine (and immunosuppression) → risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and pneumococcal/encapsulated-organism infection → penicillin prophylaxis + pneumococcal vaccination; care with live vaccines on steroids.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: Why are children with nephrotic syndrome hypercoagulable?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Loss of antithrombin III in urine + haemoconcentration → VTE, renal vein thrombosis, and rarely cerebral sinus thrombosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: List the main complications of nephrotic syndrome.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Infection (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, pneumococcus), thromboembolism (VTE/renal vein thrombosis), hypovolaemia (fluid in tissues not vessels → shock; care with diuretics), hyperlipidaemia, acute kidney injury, growth impairment/steroid side effects.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.front: How does nephritic syndrome contrast with nephrotic syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Nephrotic Syndr.back: Nephritic: haematuria + hypertension + mild proteinuria + acute kidney injury (inflammatory). Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminaemia + oedema.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions are grouped under neurodevelopmental & behavioural?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Global developmental delay and the neurodevelopmental conditions ADHD and autism spectrum disorder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the organising principle for neurodevelopmental & behavioural disorders?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Distinguish global delay (multiple domains — needs investigation) from specific patterns: ASD = social-communication + restricted/repetitive behaviours; ADHD = inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings. Assess against developmental milestones.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay across gross/fine motor, speech, social → screen for cause (hearing, vision, genetic, metabolic); MDT.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Inattention + hyperactivity/impulsivity in ≥2 settings, impairing → behavioural strategies; methylphenidate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give the features and management of autism spectrum disorder.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Persistent social-communication difficulty + restricted/repetitive behaviours → MDT diagnosis and support.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What developmental red flags warrant prompt referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Loss of skills/regression, no social smile by 8 weeks, not walking by 18 months. Always check hearing and vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: When a child fails to reach expected developmental milestones at the expected age.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does developmental delay matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Development is the paediatric equivalent of a vital sign — deviation flags underlying pathology (genetic, neurological, sensory, metabolic, environmental); early identification → early intervention improves outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the 'limit age' concept?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: The age by which a skill should have appeared; failure to reach it (not the average age) is what triggers action.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the four developmental domains?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: (1) Gross motor; (2) Fine motor & vision; (3) Speech, language & hearing; (4) Social, emotional & behavioural.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is isolated (specific) developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay in one domain (e.g. isolated speech delay) — often has a specific, sometimes reversible cause (e.g. hearing loss → speech delay).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is global developmental delay (GDD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Delay in ≥2 domains in a child <5 years (formally, ≥2 standard deviations below the mean) — suggests a broader/underlying cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is developmental regression and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Loss of previously acquired skills — a serious red flag always warranting investigation (suggests a neurodegenerative/metabolic condition, e.g. a leukodystrophy or Rett syndrome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How do you correct for prematurity when assessing development?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Subtract the weeks of prematurity from chronological age (until ~2 years): milestone age = age − weeks born early.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: By what age should a child sit without support, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Sits without support ~7–8 months; refer at 12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: By what age should a child walk unsupported, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Walks unsupported ~13–15 months; refer at 18 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the key gross-motor memory hooks '6, 9, 12'?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: 6 = sits with support, 9 = sits with no support, 12 = refer if can't sit unsupported. Also '3, 6, 9, 12 — heads, shoulders, knees and toes': 3 mo head control, 6 mo sitting (supported), 9 mo crawling, 12 mo walking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why is hand preference before 12 months abnormal?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It may indicate a contralateral hemiplegia/cerebral palsy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the speech/language limit ages for first words and 2-word phrases?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: 2–6 words by 12–15 months (refer at 18 months); combines 2 words by 2 years.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When does a baby smile, and when do you refer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Smiles at 6 weeks; refer at 10 weeks (no smile by 8–10 weeks is a red flag).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List the developmental red flags warranting referral.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Loss of any acquired skill (regression — most serious); no smile by 8–10 weeks; no eye contact by ~3 months; no reaching by 6 months; no sitting by 9–12 months; no walking by 18 months; no words by 18 months; no 2-word phrases by 2 years; hand preference before 12 months.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List genetic/antenatal causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Genetic/chromosomal: Down syndrome, Fragile X, other syndromes. Antenatal: congenital infection (TORCH), fetal alcohol syndrome, teratogens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List perinatal/postnatal causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Perinatal: prematurity, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, kernicterus. Postnatal: meningitis/encephalitis, head injury, non-accidental injury, hypothyroidism, metabolic disorders.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: List neurological, sensory and environmental causes of developmental delay.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Neurological: cerebral palsy, neuromuscular disease (e.g. Duchenne), neural tube defects. Sensory: hearing impairment (→ speech delay), visual impairment. Environmental/social: neglect, understimulation, safeguarding concerns. Often idiopathic — much isolated delay is time-limited with a good prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does assessment of developmental delay involve?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Detailed history (pregnancy/birth, milestones, family history, hearing/vision, social) + examination (growth, head circumference, neuro, dysmorphism) + development assessment; always check hearing and vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What investigations may be used in developmental delay?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Guided by findings: genetic testing (chromosomal microarray, Fragile X), TFTs, creatine kinase (if motor delay — Duchenne), metabolic screen, ± MRI/EEG.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is developmental delay managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: MDT — community paediatrics, SALT (speech), physiotherapy (gross motor), occupational therapy (fine motor), audiology, orthoptics, portage, health visitor, educational support; treat any reversible cause; safeguarding referral if neglect suspected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: A neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that is developmentally inappropriate and impairs functioning across multiple settings (home and school/work).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does ADHD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It is common (~5% of children); untreated it causes academic underachievement, low self-esteem and secondary problems (conduct disorder, anxiety, depression, substance misuse); and it is very treatable.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What makes ADHD a disorder rather than normal behaviour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Symptoms are persistent (≥6 months), present before age 12, occur in ≥2 settings, and cause real impairment — so diagnosis requires observation across settings and cannot be made on a rating scale alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the three presentations of ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Predominantly inattentive (the 'daydreamer'; easily missed, commoner in girls); predominantly hyperactive-impulsive; and combined (both — the commonest).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the DSM-5 diagnostic requirements for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Symptoms persistent for ≥6 months, onset before age 12, in ≥2 settings, causing ≥moderate impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How many symptoms are needed for ADHD by age?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Children/young people (<17 years): ≥6 features from a domain. Adults (≥17 years): ≥5 features (the threshold drops for adults).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of inattention symptoms in ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Doesn't follow through on instructions; reluctant to engage in mentally-intense tasks; easily distracted; difficulty sustaining attention; difficulty organising tasks; forgetful; loses things; doesn't seem to listen when spoken to.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms in ADHD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Unable to play quietly; talks excessively; doesn't wait their turn; leaves seat when expected to sit; often 'on the go'; interrupts/intrudes; answers prematurely; runs/climbs inappropriately.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions commonly co-occur with ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Autism spectrum disorder, oppositional defiant/conduct disorder, tic disorders/Tourette's, learning disability/dyslexia, anxiety and depression, attachment/sleep problems, epilepsy. Consider safeguarding, attachment disorder and hearing/vision as mimics.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is ADHD diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: By a specialist after a full clinical and psychosocial assessment, developmental and psychiatric history, and observer reports from ≥2 settings (e.g. school). Do NOT diagnose on rating scales or observation alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What role do rating scales play in ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Conners' rating scales and the Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) are useful adjuncts; QbTest may aid diagnosis in 6–17s — but they don't replace clinical assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is first-line management of ADHD before medication (NICE NG87)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Watchful waiting (up to 10 weeks) for mild symptoms; do NOT offer medication first-line for pre-school children — offer a group parent-training/education programme; education about ADHD, environmental modifications, sleep/diet/exercise advice; ADHD-focused group parent-training (children) and CBT (older children/adults).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Methylphenidate (a stimulant; short- or long-acting) for children ≥5 and young people, if there is persistent significant impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is second-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Lisdexamfetamine (or dexamfetamine) if a 6-week trial of methylphenidate gives insufficient benefit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the non-stimulant options for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Atomoxetine (an SNRI) or guanfacine — if stimulants are ineffective/not tolerated/contraindicated, or where diversion/misuse is a concern.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What baseline checks are needed before starting stimulants for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Measure height, weight, baseline BP and HR, and take a cardiac history (ECG if cardiac history/signs — stimulants raise HR/BP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What monitoring is required on stimulants for ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Monitor height and weight (stimulants can suppress growth/appetite — plot on centile charts) and BP/HR (every dose change and ~6-monthly). Watch for reduced appetite, insomnia, tics, mood changes; atomoxetine — monitor for suicidal ideation and hepatic toxicity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why are SSRIs/antipsychotics NOT used for core ADHD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: They describe autism/challenging-behaviour management — for ADHD itself the drug is a stimulant (methylphenidate).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is autism spectrum disorder (ASD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: A lifelong neurodevelopmental condition defined by two core domains: (1) persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, and (2) restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Why does ASD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It is common (~1–2%), early recognition and support markedly improve function and quality of life, and it is frequently missed or misattributed — especially in girls and those with normal/high intelligence.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does 'spectrum' mean in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: It spans from profound impairment with intellectual disability and no speech to highly able individuals with subtle social difficulties (formerly Asperger's, now subsumed into ASD in DSM-5) — hence variable presentation and individualised management.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What does DSM-5 require for an ASD diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Deficits in BOTH domains (the 'dyad'), present from early childhood, causing functional impairment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of social communication & interaction deficits in ASD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Poor social-emotional reciprocity (back-and-forth conversation, sharing interests/emotions); impaired non-verbal communication (reduced eye contact, gestures, facial expression); difficulty developing/maintaining relationships; lack of interest in peers; absent imaginative/shared play.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Give examples of restricted, repetitive behaviours (RRBs) in ASD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Stereotyped/repetitive movements or speech (hand-flapping, lining up toys, echolalia); insistence on sameness, inflexible routines, distress at change; highly restricted fixated interests of abnormal intensity; hyper- or hypo-reactivity to sensory input.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are the early features/red flags of ASD prompting referral (NICE CG128)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: No babble/pointing/gesture by ~12 months; no single words by 16 months; no 2-word phrases by 24 months; reduced/absent eye contact; not responding to their name; lack of protodeclarative pointing/joint attention; not showing objects to others; limited pretend play; loss of language or social skills at any age (regression); repetitive behaviours, unusual sensory responses, preference for being alone.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What conditions are associated with ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Strongly genetic/heritable (polygenic); associated with Fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, Rett syndrome, Down syndrome, fetal valproate/alcohol exposure, prematurity/SGA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Is ASD caused by the MMR vaccine?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: No — the alleged link is comprehensively discredited/fraudulent; ASD is NOT caused by MMR (a high-yield public-health point).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What are common comorbidities of ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: ADHD (very common overlap), intellectual/learning disability and specific learning difficulties, epilepsy, anxiety and depression, OCD, sleep disorders, feeding problems, tics/Tourette's, motor coordination difficulties (dyspraxia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: How is ASD diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Clinically and multidisciplinarily (a specialist 'autism team') — detailed developmental history + observation across settings (home + school), against DSM-5 criteria; there is no single diagnostic blood test or scan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What structured tools support ASD diagnosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: ADOS (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule) and ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) — they support but don't replace clinical judgement. Assess for comorbidities and check hearing and vision; consider genetic testing where indicated.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: What is the core/first-line management of ASD (NICE CG170)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: There is no cure — management is support-based, individualised and MDT-led. Psychosocial/behavioural interventions are the foundation: a play-based intervention with parents/carers/teachers to increase joint attention, engagement and reciprocal communication; SALT, occupational therapy (incl. sensory strategies), educational support/EHCP, structured/predictable environments, parent/carer training and family support.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: Does any medication treat the core features of ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: No — no medication treats the core social-communication/RRB features; medication is only for comorbidities/challenging behaviour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When are antipsychotics used in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: Specialist use for behaviour that challenges (aggression, self-injury) — e.g. risperidone/aripiprazole; review at 3–4 weeks, stop by 6 weeks if no benefit.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.front: When are SSRIs and methylphenidate used in ASD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neurodevelopmen.back: SSRIs — for comorbid anxiety, depression or OCD/repetitive behaviours (specialist, cautiously). Methylphenidate — for comorbid ADHD. Also treat epilepsy and sleep disorders (e.g. melatonin).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How do inherited neuromuscular disorders impair movement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: By affecting the muscle itself (the muscular dystrophies) or the motor neuron/lower motor unit (spinal muscular atrophy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Which four inherited neuromuscular disorders are needed for finals?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The two dystrophinopathies (Duchenne, Becker), myotonic dystrophy, and spinal muscular atrophy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive; no dystrophin (Xp21). Boy ~2–5 yrs, proximal weakness, Gower's sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, huge CK.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of Becker muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive; partial dystrophin (in-frame). Same picture as DMD but milder + later; prominent cardiomyopathy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of myotonic dystrophy (DM1).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Autosomal dominant; CTG repeat (DMPK); anticipation. Myotonia (can't release grip) + distal weakness, frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Give the genetics and hallmark of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Autosomal recessive; SMN1 deletion (a motor-neuron disease, NOT a dystrophy). Floppy baby, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, preserved intellect.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the key framing distinguishing these disorders?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dystrophies are primary muscle diseases (proximal weakness, high CK) — except myotonic dystrophy which is distal + multisystem. SMA is a lower-motor-neuron disease (anterior horn cell) → floppy, areflexic, with fasciculations.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A severe, progressive, X-linked recessive muscle-wasting disease caused by a near-total absence of dystrophin — a structural protein anchoring the muscle-cell membrane to the internal cytoskeleton.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why does DMD matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: It is the commonest and most severe inherited muscular dystrophy of childhood (~1 in 3500–5000 male births), following a relentless course (walking → wheelchair by ~teens → death from cardiorespiratory failure in the 20s–30s); early recognition enables surveillance + steroid treatment that alter the course.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of DMD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The dystrophin gene (Xp21) is the largest human gene. DMD = a frameshift/nonsense mutation → NO functional dystrophin → muscle-membrane fragility → repeated damage → necrosis → replacement by fat and fibrous tissue.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does the mutation type differ between Duchenne and Becker?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Duchenne: frameshift → NO dystrophin (severe). Becker: in-frame mutation → some partial dystrophin (milder, later). The amount of residual dystrophin determines severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the inheritance of DMD and who is affected?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: X-linked recessive → affects boys; mothers are usually carriers (may have raised CK/mild cardiomyopathy). ~1/3 are new (de novo) mutations with no family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the presentation of DMD.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Progressive proximal muscle weakness from ~2–5 years — delayed walking, frequent falls, difficulty climbing stairs/running, waddling gait, difficulty getting up off the floor.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Gower's sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The child 'walks his hands up his legs' to stand from squatting/the floor — due to proximal hip/thigh weakness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is calf pseudohypertrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Enlarged calves from fat/fibrous replacement of muscle — looks bulky but is weak.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What proportion of DMD boys have intellectual impairment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: ~30% have intellectual impairment/learning difficulty.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What are the later musculoskeletal features of DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Loss of ambulation, contractures, scoliosis, respiratory muscle weakness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the leading cardiac complication of DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy → heart failure, arrhythmias (the most common association).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the commonest cause of death in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Respiratory failure (with cardiomyopathy) — progressive respiratory-muscle weakness → nocturnal hypoventilation, recurrent chest infections.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the key screening investigation in a boy with weakness suggesting DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Markedly raised creatine kinase (CK) — often 10–100x normal.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing (dystrophin gene deletion/duplication/point mutation — MLPA + sequencing), replacing muscle biopsy in most cases. Biopsy (if genetics inconclusive) shows absent dystrophin on immunostaining (vs reduced in Becker).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What surveillance investigations are used in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Echocardiography/cardiac MRI + ECG (cardiomyopathy) and lung function/spirometry.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the disease-modifying mainstay of DMD management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Corticosteroids (prednisolone/deflazacort) — slow the decline and prolong ambulation; monitor weight gain, osteoporosis, growth suppression. Vamorolone is a newer steroid with a better side-effect profile.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What mutation-specific therapies exist for DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides (eteplirsen — exon-51-skippable mutations), ataluren (nonsense mutations), and gene therapy (micro-dystrophin, e.g. delandistrogene moxeparvovec) — evolving, availability varies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What organ-protection and support are used in DMD?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac: ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers for the dilated cardiomyopathy (started early/prophylactically). Respiratory: monitoring, non-invasive ventilation, cough assist, chest physio, vaccinations. MDT: physiotherapy, OT, orthotics, scoliosis surgery, bone health, nutrition, psychology, education.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A milder, later-onset X-linked muscle-wasting disease caused by a partial deficiency of dystrophin — the same protein and gene as Duchenne, but with some partially-functional dystrophin preserved.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the relationship between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: They are allelic (same-gene) counterparts on a severity spectrum set by how much functional dystrophin remains.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the 'reading-frame rule'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: In-frame mutations keep the reading frame → shortened but partially functional dystrophin → milder Becker; frameshift/out-of-frame mutations → no functional dystrophin → severe Duchenne. Residual dystrophin sets the severity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How do onset and progression differ between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Becker: later onset (~5–15 yrs, up to adulthood), slower progression, often walking into 40s+. Duchenne: onset ~2–5 yrs, rapid progression, wheelchair by early teens.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does cognition and survival differ between Becker and Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Becker: cognition usually normal, near-normal/later adulthood survival. Duchenne: ~30% cognitive impairment, survival 20s–30s.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is a useful clinical rule of thumb distinguishing Becker from Duchenne?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A boy still walking after age 16 = Becker; wheelchair-bound before 13 = Duchenne. Between those, genetic testing settles it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the clinical features of Becker muscular dystrophy.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Progressive proximal weakness (legs/pelvic girdle first, like DMD but later + milder) — difficulty running, climbing stairs, getting up; later trunk/upper limbs; calf pseudohypertrophy; Gower's sign may be present; muscle cramps on exertion are relatively characteristic.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What can be the first/presenting sign of Becker muscular dystrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac involvement — dilated cardiomyopathy may appear (and be severe) even when skeletal weakness is mild.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is often the leading cause of death in Becker muscular dystrophy?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Dilated cardiomyopathy — as the skeletal disease is milder, the heart becomes the limiting problem; also arrhythmias/conduction defects.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why do female carriers of Becker need cardiac screening?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: They can develop dilated cardiomyopathy (and have mildly raised CK).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How is Becker muscular dystrophy investigated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Raised CK (high, though generally less extreme than DMD); definitive = genetic testing (identifies the in-frame mutation); biopsy shows reduced/patchy dystrophin (vs absent in DMD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is central to Becker muscular dystrophy management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac surveillance (echocardiography/cardiac MRI + ECG) and cardiac protection with ACE inhibitors ± beta-blockers, given the cardiac burden; supportive MDT (physiotherapy, OT, orthotics); steroids used more selectively than in DMD; genetic counselling + cardiac screening of female carriers.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: The commonest adult-onset muscular dystrophy — an autosomal dominant, multisystem disorder caused by a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK gene.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What three exam-defining features set DM1 apart from the other dystrophies?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: It is autosomal dominant (not X-linked); it causes myotonia (delayed relaxation) with DISTAL rather than proximal weakness; and it is multisystem — so cardiac and respiratory complications (not the weakness) are what kill. It is the classic example of genetic anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: An unstable CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the 3′-untranslated region of DMPK (chromosome 19) produces a toxic RNA that disrupts RNA splicing across many tissues → the multisystem picture. The repeat expands in successive generations → earlier onset + more severe disease = anticipation (normal <~34 repeats; disease >~50; congenital >~1000–2000).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is myotonia, the hallmark of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Delayed muscle relaxation after contraction — e.g. can't quickly let go of a handshake/grip ('grip myotonia'), or a percussion dimple slow to relax; it warms up (improves) with repeated use.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the muscle (distal) pattern of DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Distal weakness first (hand grip, foot drop); facial weakness → long, thin 'hatchet'/myopathic face, ptosis, wasted temples/masseters, weak neck flexors; dysphagia, dysarthria (bulbar involvement).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What are the multisystem features of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cataracts (early, posterior subcapsular); cardiac conduction defects & arrhythmias (heart block, AF; risk of sudden death); frontal balding (esp. men); insulin resistance/diabetes; testicular atrophy/hypogonadism; excessive daytime sleepiness; mild cognitive impairment; respiratory-muscle weakness; constipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe congenital DM1.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Almost always inherited from an affected MOTHER (very large repeat expansions); presents at birth with severe hypotonia ('floppy infant'), facial diplegia, feeding/respiratory difficulty, talipes, and later intellectual disability; high neonatal mortality — a key example of anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing — detects the DMPK CTG-repeat expansion (length roughly correlates with severity/onset).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the CK level in DM1, and why is this useful?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Normal or mildly raised — unlike the very high CK of DMD/BMD, a useful distinguishing point.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What EMG finding is characteristic of DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: 'Dive-bomber'/myotonic discharges (waxing-waning).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What other investigations are used in DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: ECG (essential — conduction defects; regular surveillance), echocardiography; slit-lamp (cataracts), glucose/HbA1c, sleep/respiratory assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the most important intervention in DM1 management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Cardiac surveillance — annual ECG (± Holter/echo); pacemaker/ICD for significant conduction disease/arrhythmia (reduces sudden death).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Why is anaesthetic caution vital in DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: DM1 patients are highly sensitive to anaesthetic agents + opioids (respiratory depression, prolonged apnoea, arrhythmia) → specialist anaesthetic care; flag before surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How is troublesome myotonia and other DM1 problems managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Myotonia → mexiletine (sodium-channel blocker); physiotherapy/OT, orthotics (foot drop); modafinil for hypersomnia; treat diabetes; cataract surgery; respiratory support (NIV); dysphagia/aspiration management; genetic counselling (autosomal dominant, anticipation, congenital-form risk via maternal transmission).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does DM2 differ from DM1?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: DM2 is a milder, purely adult, proximal variant — a CCTG repeat in CNBP/ZNF9 (chromosome 3); no congenital form, no clear anticipation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: An autosomal recessive motor neuron disease in which the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord degenerate → progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness and wasting. It is NOT a muscular dystrophy — the lesion is in the NERVE (anterior horn cell), not the muscle.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the core mechanism of SMA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Homozygous loss of the SMN1 gene (survival motor neuron 1, chromosome 5) → deficient SMN protein → degeneration of anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) → the muscle loses its nerve supply → denervation atrophy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the role of the SMN2 gene in SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: A near-identical back-up gene makes ~10–15% functional protein — so MORE SMN2 copies → MILDER disease (explains the type 0–4 spectrum and is the target of every modern therapy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: How does SMA differ from muscular dystrophy in lesion, reflexes and CK?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: SMA: lesion in the anterior horn cell (motor neuron), neurogenic, areflexia, tongue fasciculations, normal/mildly raised CK, no pseudohypertrophy, normal cognition. Dystrophy: lesion in the muscle fibre, myopathic, reflexes reduced late, very high CK (DMD), calf pseudohypertrophy, ~30% cognitive impairment (DMD).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe the 'floppy infant' clinical features of SMA.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness + hypotonia (legs > arms); areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes — key sign of the lower motor neuron lesion); tongue fasciculations (hallmark of anterior horn cell disease); weak cry, poor feeding/swallow; 'bell-shaped chest' with paradoxical (abdominal) breathing in severe forms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is preserved in SMA despite the weakness?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Normal cognition + a bright, alert, expressive face (the child is mentally normal, 'trapped' in a weak body); no pseudohypertrophy; sensation and sphincters intact.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Onset <6 months; NEVER SITS; commonest; historically death <2 yrs (respiratory).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 2 (intermediate).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Onset 6–18 months; SITS but never walks; survival into adulthood.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Onset >18 months; WALKS (may lose it); near-normal lifespan.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: Describe SMA types 0 and 4.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Type 0: prenatal onset; never sits; very severe, death in days–weeks. Type 4: adulthood onset; walks; mildest, slow progression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the memory aid for the SMA subtypes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Type 1 never Sits, Type 2 Sits, Type 3 Stands/walks, Type 4 adult. More SMN2 copies → higher type number → milder.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the definitive diagnostic test for SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Genetic testing — homozygous SMN1 deletion/mutation; SMN2 copy number is prognostic (guides severity/treatment).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What is the CK in SMA and what other tests are used?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: CK normal or mildly raised (helps distinguish from the very high CK of DMD); EMG/nerve conduction show a neurogenic pattern (largely replaced by genetics); newborn screening increasingly detects SMA presymptomatically → early treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What disease-modifying therapies exist for SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: All raise SMN protein: nusinersen (Spinraza — intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide modifying SMN2 splicing); onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma — one-off IV gene therapy delivering a working SMN1 gene via AAV9); risdiplam (oral SMN2-splicing modifier). Earlier treatment = better outcome (before motor neurons are lost).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.front: What supportive/MDT care is essential in SMA?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Neuromuscular D.back: Respiratory (main threat): NIV, cough assist, chest physio, secretion management, vaccination (respiratory failure = leading cause of death in severe types); nutrition (feeding support/gastrostomy, aspiration prevention); physiotherapy/OT, orthotics, wheelchairs; scoliosis surgery; contracture prevention; genetic counselling (autosomal recessive — carrier testing; 1-in-4 recurrence risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the commonest childhood malignancies covered in this topic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Leukaemia (commonest overall) plus the classic solid tumours neuroblastoma, Wilms' and retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric cancers?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Presentation by tumour: ALL = marrow failure (pallor, bruising, infection) ± bone pain; abdominal mass in a young child → Wilms' (renal) or neuroblastoma (adrenal/sympathetic chain); white pupillary reflex → retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone marrow; pallor, bruising/petechiae, infections, bone pain; the commonest childhood cancer.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for neuroblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neural crest (adrenal/sympathetic); abdominal mass crossing the midline, <5yr; raised catecholamines.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for Wilms' tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Kidney; unilateral mass (doesn't cross midline), haematuria; don't repeatedly palpate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Give the origin and clue for retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Retina; leukocoria (white reflex), squint; hereditary (RB1).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What findings should prompt urgent action for possible childhood cancer?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Unexplained pallor/bruising/persistent bone pain → check FBC + blood film for leukaemia. A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) or new squint → urgent ophthalmology for retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant proliferation of immature lymphoid precursor cells (lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does ALL matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest childhood cancer (~80% of childhood leukaemias); its presentation is a bone-marrow-failure picture; and it is one of oncology's great success stories, with cure rates now ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of ALL.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A lymphoid precursor acquires mutations → clonal proliferation of lymphoblasts that crowd out normal haematopoiesis → failure of the three cell lines (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) plus infiltration of other tissues (bone, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, CNS, testes).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the commonest lineage of childhood ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: B-cell precursor (B-ALL); a minority is T-cell (T-ALL).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the peak age and key association of ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Peak incidence 2–5 years; markedly increased risk in Down syndrome (also Fanconi anaemia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Li-Fraumeni; ionising radiation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the marrow-failure triad of ALL?
