conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Anaemia → lethargy, pallor (± breathlessness); neutropenia → frequent/severe infections; thrombocytopenia → easy bruising, petechiae (± bleeding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What infiltration/systemic features occur in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone pain (a child who won't weight-bear/limps), hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, fever (up to 50%), testicular enlargement, CNS involvement (headache, cranial nerve palsies), mediastinal mass (especially T-ALL → SVC obstruction/respiratory distress).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the red-flag rule for ALL referral?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Unexplained pallor + bruising/petechiae + recurrent infection ± bone pain + hepatosplenomegaly → urgent same-day FBC + blood film + specialist referral. NICE: any child with unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly warrants immediate referral.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What FBC and blood film findings occur in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: FBC — anaemia, thrombocytopenia; WCC may be low, normal or very high; often pancytopenia with circulating blasts. Blood film — lymphoblasts (the key finding).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the diagnostic test for ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone marrow aspirate & trephine biopsy — >20% blasts confirms acute leukaemia; sent for immunophenotyping (flow cytometry) and cytogenetics/molecular studies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Which cytogenetic findings carry a good vs poor prognosis in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Good: hyperdiploidy and ETV6-RUNX1 t(12;21). Poor: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) BCR-ABL, KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement, hypodiploidy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why is a lumbar puncture done in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: To assess central-nervous-system involvement (blasts in CSF).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What baseline blood chemistry is checked in ALL and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Urate, potassium, phosphate, calcium, renal function (baseline for tumour lysis); LDH; coagulation; LFTs. Plus CXR for a mediastinal mass (T-ALL).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What two emergencies must be stabilised first in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neutropenic sepsis → immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (within 1 hour); tumour lysis syndrome → hyperhydration + allopurinol or rasburicase, monitor/correct ↑potassium, ↑phosphate, ↑urate, ↓calcium (risk of AKI/arrhythmia as blasts lyse).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the mainstay of ALL treatment and its phases?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Chemotherapy over ~2–3 years: induction (achieve remission) → consolidation/intensification → CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal chemo ± cranial irradiation — CNS/testes are sanctuary sites) → maintenance (prolonged, lower-intensity).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How is Philadelphia-positive ALL treated?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Add a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib/dasatinib).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What newer therapies exist for relapsed/refractory ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Immunotherapy — blinatumomab (bispecific), inotuzumab, and CAR-T cell therapy (tisagenlecleucel); allogeneic stem cell transplant for high-risk/relapsed disease; minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring guides risk and treatment intensity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the cure rate and the good prognostic factors in childhood ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Cure rate ~90%. Good: age 2–10 years, low WCC at diagnosis, B-cell precursor, favourable cytogenetics (hyperdiploidy, ETV6-RUNX1), rapid response/low MRD, no CNS disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the poor prognostic factors in ALL?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Age <1 or >10, high WCC (>50), T-cell, Philadelphia chromosome/hypodiploidy/KMT2A, CNS involvement at diagnosis, slow response/high MRD, male sex.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant embryonal tumour of the sympathetic nervous system, arising from primitive neural crest cells.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does neuroblastoma matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest extracranial solid tumour of childhood and the commonest cancer in infancy; a classic exam contrast with Wilms tumour; and it has an extraordinary biological spectrum from spontaneous regression in infants to aggressive disease in older children.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Where does neuroblastoma arise?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Anywhere sympathetic tissue exists — most commonly the adrenal medulla (~50%), but also the paravertebral sympathetic chain (neck→pelvis). Because these cells produce catecholamines, the tumour often secretes them → raised urinary VMA/HVA.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How does neuroblastoma contrast with Wilms tumour in origin, age and the child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neuroblastoma: sympathetic chain/adrenal medulla (neural crest), <5yr median ~18 months, often systemically unwell (metastatic at diagnosis ~50–60%). Wilms: kidney (metanephric blastema), peak 3–4 yr, often a well child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How does the abdominal mass differ between neuroblastoma and Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neuroblastoma: irregular, hard, CROSSES the midline. Wilms: smooth, confined to one side, rarely crosses midline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What tumour markers and key genetics distinguish neuroblastoma from Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Neuroblastoma: raised urinary catecholamines (VMA/HVA); MYCN amplification (poor prognosis). Wilms: usually no markers; WT1/WT2, WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the exam one-liner for neuroblastoma vs Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An unwell young child with a hard abdominal mass crossing the midline + bone pain + raised urinary VMA → neuroblastoma; a well child with a smooth flank mass not crossing the midline → Wilms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the commonest presentation of neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An abdominal mass — firm, irregular, non-tender, may cross the midline; plus systemic features (weight loss, malaise, fever, pallor — often looks unwell).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What features come from bone-marrow metastases in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bone pain, limp, pancytopenia — can mimic leukaemia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is a classic sign of orbital/skull metastases in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes') and proptosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What site-specific features can neuroblastoma cause?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Thoracic tumour → respiratory symptoms; paraspinal tumour → cord compression (dumbbell extension through the intervertebral foramen); cervical tumour → Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What catecholamine and paraneoplastic effects occur in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Catecholamine effects: hypertension, sweating, flushing, secretory diarrhoea (VIP). Paraneoplastic: opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia ('dancing eyes, dancing feet' — immune-mediated, paradoxically good prognosis); VIP secretion → intractable watery diarrhoea.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the key biochemical test for neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Urinary catecholamine metabolites — VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and HVA (homovanillic acid) raised in ~90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What imaging is used in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Ultrasound (initial abdominal mass) → CT/MRI (extent, staging); MIBG scan (taken up by sympathetic/catecholaminergic tissue) for the tumour and metastases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What does neuroblastoma biopsy show, and what molecular testing is done?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Histology: small round blue cells, ± Homer-Wright rosettes; molecular testing including MYCN amplification, ALK, and chromosomal changes (1p/11q loss). Also bone marrow aspirate/trephine (marrow involvement common); FBC, LDH, ferritin (raised = adverse).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: How is neuroblastoma treatment risk-stratified?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: INRG: age, stage, histology, MYCN, ploidy. Low-risk/infant → observation (may spontaneously regress, especially stage 4S infants) or surgery alone; intermediate-risk → surgery + moderate chemotherapy; high-risk → intensive multimodal therapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the high-risk neuroblastoma treatment sequence?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Induction chemotherapy → surgery → high-dose chemo + autologous stem cell rescue → radiotherapy → maintenance with immunotherapy (anti-GD2 monoclonal antibody, e.g. dinutuximab) + retinoic acid.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What are the good and poor prognostic factors in neuroblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Good: infants <18 months, localised disease, favourable histology, hyperdiploidy, no MYCN amplification, opsoclonus-myoclonus. Poor: MYCN amplification, age >18 months, metastatic (high-risk) disease, 1p/11q loss (high-risk survival only ~50%).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What unique feature can occur in some infant neuroblastomas?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Some infant tumours (stage 4S) regress spontaneously without treatment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Wilms tumour (nephroblastoma)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant embryonal tumour of the kidney, arising from primitive metanephric blastema (the embryonic tissue that forms the kidney).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does Wilms tumour matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the commonest renal malignancy of childhood (and commonest paediatric abdominal cancer), the classic exam contrast with neuroblastoma, and a modern oncology success story with cure rates >85–90%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of Wilms tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Metanephric blastema fails to differentiate and proliferates, producing a triphasic tumour (blastemal + epithelial + stromal elements). Mutations in WT1/WT2 (chromosome 11) underlie the syndromic forms.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the age and laterality of Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Typically <5 years, peak 3–4 years (slightly older than neuroblastoma); usually unilateral, bilateral in ~5–10%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is WAGR syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, Retardation (intellectual disability); associated with WT1 deletion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and its link to Wilms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An overgrowth syndrome — macrosomia, macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihypertrophy, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycaemia — associated with Wilms tumour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is Denys-Drash syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Nephropathy + genitourinary malformation + Wilms (~90% develop Wilms). (Also isolated hemihypertrophy is associated.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the classic clinical stem for Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: An asymptomatic abdominal mass discovered incidentally (by a parent bathing the child, or on routine exam).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the abdominal mass of Wilms tumour.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Large, smooth, firm, unilateral, does not cross the midline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What other clinical features occur in Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Painless haematuria; flank/abdominal pain; anorexia, fever, malaise; hypertension (from renin secretion/renal artery compression — a classic feature); rarely rapid enlargement/pain after minor trauma (haemorrhage into tumour).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the referral rule for an unexplained abdominal mass in a child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Paediatric review within 48 hours (NICE NG12).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the initial investigation for Wilms tumour, and what follows?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Abdominal ultrasound (confirms a renal-origin mass) → CT/MRI abdomen & chest for staging (local extent, contralateral kidney, lung metastases — the commonest site).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What does Wilms tumour histology show?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Triphasic: epithelial tubules, immature glomerular structures, stroma with spindle cells, and small-cell blastematous tissue resembling metanephric blastema, ± necrosis. (In the European/SIOP approach, chemotherapy is often given before biopsy/surgery based on imaging.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the mainstay of Wilms tumour treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Nephrectomy — surgical removal of the tumour and affected kidney.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the role of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Chemotherapy — often neoadjuvant (before surgery, standard in the European/SIOP protocol) and/or adjuvant after surgery. Radiotherapy — for advanced/higher-stage or unfavourable-histology disease. Bilateral disease → nephron-sparing surgery where possible.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the prognosis of Wilms tumour?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Excellent — overall survival >85–90% (favourable histology, localised); worse with anaplastic (unfavourable) histology, higher stage, or metastatic disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A malignant tumour of the developing retina — the commonest intraocular/ocular malignancy of childhood.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why does retinoblastoma matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: It is the classic paradigm of the 'two-hit hypothesis' of tumour-suppressor genes; its hallmark sign leukocoria is detectable on the routine red-reflex check (so early detection saves sight and life); and the hereditary form predisposes to bilateral disease and second cancers.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe the core mechanism of retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: RB1 (chromosome 13q14) is a tumour-suppressor gene whose protein (pRb) restrains the cell cycle; retinoblastoma requires inactivation of BOTH copies of RB1 (Knudson's two-hit hypothesis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe hereditary retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: ~40% — a germline RB1 mutation is inherited (the 'first hit' is in every cell) → only one further somatic hit is needed → tumours arise early, bilaterally and multifocally, with lifelong risk of second malignancies (especially osteosarcoma).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Describe sporadic retinoblastoma.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: ~60% — both hits are somatic in a single retinal cell → usually unilateral, unifocal, later onset.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the age at diagnosis of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Average ~18 months; nearly all <5 years (bilateral present earlier, ~1 yr; unilateral ~2 yr).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the inheritance of hereditary retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Autosomal dominant (germline mutation, high penetrance) — all bilateral (and multifocal) cases are hereditary. Tumour formation is 'recessive at the cellular level' (needing both alleles hit).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is leukocoria and its significance in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: A white pupillary reflex / absent (or white) red reflex — the commonest and most important sign; often first noticed as a white pupil in flash photographs.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the second commonest presentation of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Strabismus (squint) — the tumour impairs vision so the eye deviates. Any child with a new squint needs fundoscopy to exclude retinoblastoma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What other/advanced features occur in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Deteriorating/loss of vision, a red or painful eye, a change in eye appearance; advanced: proptosis, orbital inflammation, buphthalmos (enlarged eye). May be picked up on routine red-reflex screening (newborn & 6-week checks) or family screening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the key diagnostic assessment for retinoblastoma, and what is avoided?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with dilated fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist. Biopsy is AVOIDED (risk of seeding tumour outside the eye) — diagnosis is clinical/imaging-based when confined to the eye.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What imaging is used in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Ocular ultrasound (often shows calcification) and MRI (extent, optic nerve/CNS involvement — avoid CT to limit radiation, especially in hereditary cases).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: Why is RB1 genetic testing essential in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: To identify hereditary disease → screen the child's siblings/relatives and future offspring, and guide surveillance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the order of treatment priorities in retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Save life → save the eye → preserve vision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What treatments are used for retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Focal/local therapies for small tumours (laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy, thermotherapy, plaque brachytherapy); chemotherapy — systemic (carboplatin, vincristine, etoposide) or intra-arterial/intravitreal to salvage the eye; enucleation for advanced/large tumours with no useful vision (a prosthesis is fitted); external-beam radiotherapy reserved and avoided where possible in hereditary disease (raises second-cancer/osteosarcoma risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is the prognosis and follow-up of retinoblastoma?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Excellent — ~90% survive into adulthood in high-income countries; worse with extraocular/optic nerve/CNS spread or metastasis. Hereditary survivors need lifelong surveillance for second malignancies (especially osteosarcoma, also soft-tissue sarcomas, melanoma), heightened by radiotherapy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.front: What is 'trilateral retinoblastoma'?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Canc.back: Bilateral retinoblastoma + an intracranial (pineal) tumour — a rare, serious hereditary association.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the organising principle for the painful/limping child?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Age is the key discriminator for the painful/limping hip: DDH (neonatal screen); Perthes (4–8yr, avascular necrosis); SUFE (adolescent, often overweight); Osgood-Schlatter (adolescent knee, overuse).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Neonate; Barlow/Ortolani, ultrasound; harness or surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for Perthes disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 4–8yr (boys); avascular necrosis of femoral head; painless limp; X-ray.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for SUFE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 10–16yr, overweight; hip/knee pain, externally rotated leg; surgical pinning.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Give the age and clue for Osgood-Schlatter disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Adolescent; anterior knee pain/tibial tuberosity swelling, overuse; self-limiting.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What should you always do in a child presenting with knee pain, and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Always examine the hip — an adolescent with hip or referred knee pain and an externally rotated leg → think SUFE (urgent fixation; avoid weight-bearing).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip joint — from a shallow/dysplastic acetabulum, through a subluxatable/dislocatable hip, to a frankly dislocated hip.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does DDH matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is common (~1–3% of newborns have some instability); early detection and simple treatment (a harness) give excellent outcomes, whereas late diagnosis means surgery and lifelong consequences (limp, pain, early osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis) — hence UK newborn screening (NIPE).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core concept of hip development in DDH.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The hip must develop congruently — a well-seated femoral head stimulates the acetabulum to deepen. If the head sits abnormally, the acetabulum stays shallow, worsening the problem (a vicious cycle). Early reduction and holding the hip flexed/abducted (Pavlik harness) allows normal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the strongest risk factor for DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Breech presentation (especially breech at/after 36 weeks, or breech at delivery).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: List the risk factors for DDH.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Breech (strongest), female sex (~6:1), family history (first-degree relative), firstborn, oligohydramnios, macrosomia, multiple pregnancy; left hip most commonly affected; associated packaging disorders (talipes, torticollis, plagiocephaly) and laxity syndromes (Down, Ehlers-Danlos).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is DDH screened in the UK?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: NIPE — a newborn hip exam (<72 h) and a repeat at the 6–8-week check; ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks for breech (at/after 36 weeks or at delivery), first-degree family history, or an abnormal/uncertain clinical exam.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the Ortolani test.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Relocates a dislocated hip: with hips/knees flexed, abduct and lift the femur → a palpable 'clunk' as the head reduces into the acetabulum ('Ortolani = Open out, back In').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the Barlow test.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Dislocates a dislocatable hip: adduct the flexed hip and apply gentle posterior pressure → the head slips out posteriorly ('Barlow = pushes Back').

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the significance of a 'clunk' vs a 'click' in DDH examination?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A 'clunk' (relocation/dislocation) is significant; a 'click' is usually benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the other/later signs of DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Limited/asymmetrical hip abduction (a key sign, especially after the neonatal period); asymmetrical skin/thigh/gluteal creases; leg-length discrepancy — Galeazzi sign (knees at different heights when hips/knees flexed, feet flat); later (walking age): painless limp, waddling/Trendelenburg gait (if bilateral), toe-walking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the imaging of choice for DDH and why?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Ultrasound under ~4.5–6 months (the femoral head is not yet ossified, so X-ray is unreliable) — assesses acetabular morphology and head position; Graf classification grades severity. X-ray (pelvis) from ~4.5–6 months onward once the femoral head ossifies.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the timing pitfall in DDH ultrasound?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Ultrasound too early (first few weeks) over-detects transient laxity — hence screening ultrasound at ~4–6 weeks; many mild cases/neonatal instability resolve spontaneously.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is first-line management for DDH in infants <6 months?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Pavlik harness — a dynamic splint holding the hips flexed and abducted, allowing normal acetabular development; worn continuously for several weeks (~6–12), with regular ultrasound monitoring. Avoid forced/full abduction (risk of avascular necrosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is DDH managed in older infants (>6 months) or after failed harness?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Surgery — closed reduction (± adductor tenotomy) and hip spica cast, or open reduction ± acetabular/femoral osteotomy for late/severe cases; follow-up to ensure normal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the complications of DDH?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (from untreated DDH or over-aggressive splinting); persistent dysplasia/subluxation, leg-length discrepancy, gait abnormality; early (premature) osteoarthritis of the hip (the major long-term consequence of missed/late DDH); redislocation, need for repeat surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Idiopathic avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head in a child — the blood supply to the developing femoral epiphysis is temporarily disrupted, the bone dies, collapses, then slowly revascularises and remodels.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does Perthes disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is a key cause of the limping child, the classic 'painless limp in a young school-age boy'; although self-healing, the shape the femoral head heals into determines lifelong hip function (a flattened, deformed head → early osteoarthritis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of Perthes disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The femoral head's blood supply in this age group is precarious (largely via the lateral epiphyseal vessels, little collateral). An interruption → osteonecrosis of the epiphysis; the dead bone is weak → collapses/fragments under weight-bearing, then is resorbed and replaced (revascularisation/remodelling) over months–years. Treatment aims to keep the softened head well-seated ('contained') so it remodels round.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the classic age and sex of Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Age 4–8 years (range ~2–12); boys ~4–5:1; usually unilateral, bilateral ~10–15%.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What does bilateral Perthes disease warrant?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Investigation for multiple epiphyseal dysplasia / hypothyroidism / sickle cell — it shouldn't be symmetrical Perthes. Perthes is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out sickle cell, leukaemia, steroids, Gaucher's).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How does Perthes differ from SUFE and transient synovitis by age/habitus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Perthes: 4–8yr, small/active, insidious painless limp. SUFE: 10–15yr, overweight, hip/knee pain. Transient synovitis: 3–10yr, any habitus, acute after viral illness. All are systemically well — an unwell/febrile child needs septic arthritis excluded first (Kocher criteria).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Painless or mildly painful limp, insidious over weeks–months; hip, groin, thigh or referred KNEE pain; worse with activity, better with rest; no systemic upset (afebrile, well); restricted hip movement (especially abduction and internal rotation); antalgic gait, later Trendelenburg gait, thigh/gluteal wasting from disuse.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the first-line investigation for Perthes disease and its evolving findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: X-ray of both hips (AP + frog-leg lateral). Findings evolve: early widened joint space → increased density/sclerosis and a smaller epiphysis → subchondral fracture/'crescent sign' → fragmentation → flattening/collapse → remodelling (Waldenström stages).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the role of MRI and bloods in Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: MRI — more sensitive for early disease (before X-ray changes) and to assess necrosis extent. Bloods (FBC, CRP/ESR) — normal in Perthes; used to exclude septic arthritis/infection/malignancy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the guiding principle of Perthes management?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Containment — keep the femoral head deep in the acetabulum so it remodels spherically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Perthes managed in younger children (<6 years) with limited involvement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Conservative: observation, activity restriction, physiotherapy (maintain range of movement, especially abduction), analgesia, and monitoring — most remodel well (years of growth left); restricted weight-bearing/abduction bracing/casting in selected cases.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Perthes managed in older children (>6–8 years) or severe involvement?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Surgery — femoral or pelvic (Salter) osteotomy to re-contain and re-orient the head; long-term follow-up; total hip replacement may eventually be needed if the head heals poorly.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the good and poor prognostic factors in Perthes disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Good: younger age at onset (more remodelling potential; children <6 often do very well). Poor: older age (>8), female sex, more of the head involved (lateral pillar/Herring classification), greater deformity at healing. Main long-term risk: premature osteoarthritis (from a non-spherical head).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is slipped upper femoral epiphysis (SUFE/SCFE)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis relative to the metaphysis through the growth plate (physis) — the femoral neck slips anteriorly and rotates externally, while the femoral head stays seated in the acetabulum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does SUFE matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence, is frequently missed (up to ~50% at first presentation — classically because it presents with knee pain, not hip pain), and delayed diagnosis dramatically raises the risk of avascular necrosis and lifelong hip disability.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of SUFE.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: During the adolescent growth spurt the physis is at its weakest and under high shear; excess load (obesity) and/or hormonal factors overwhelm it → the epiphysis 'slips' — essentially a Salter-Harris type I fracture through the growth plate occurring atraumatically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the classic patient and age for SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Age 10–15 years (boys ~13, girls ~12, around the growth spurt); boys ~2–3:1; the classic 'overweight adolescent male'.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the strongest modifiable risk factor for SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Obesity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What endocrine associations should prompt screening in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency/treatment, panhypopituitarism; also renal osteodystrophy, vitamin D deficiency. Screen for endocrine disease if the child is young (<10), underweight, or has bilateral slips. Bilateral in ~20–40% (often sequential).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Hip, groin, thigh or classically KNEE pain (referred; ~25–50% present with knee/thigh pain, hip pain may be absent in up to half); limp (antalgic), reduced weight-bearing; sub-acute/chronic onset over weeks, sometimes acute-on-chronic after minor trauma.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the most reliable examination sign in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The affected leg is held in EXTERNAL rotation, with loss of internal rotation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Drehmann's sign?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Obligatory external rotation of the hip as it is passively flexed — highly characteristic of SUFE.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What X-ray views are used for SUFE, and which is most sensitive?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: X-ray of BOTH hips — AP AND frog-leg lateral views; the frog-leg lateral is the most sensitive (a subtle slip may be invisible on AP).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Trethowan's sign / Klein's line?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A line along the superior border of the femoral neck should normally intersect part of the epiphysis; in SUFE it doesn't (epiphysis slips below it) — the 'melting ice-cream cone/scoop' appearance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is SUFE classified, and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Stable (can weight-bear, ± crutches) vs unstable (cannot weight-bear even with crutches) — unstable slips carry a much higher risk of avascular necrosis (the key prognostic split). Also graded by chronicity and magnitude.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the immediate management of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Make the child NON-WEIGHT-BEARING and refer to orthopaedics urgently (further slipping worsens outcome).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the surgical mainstay of SUFE treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: 'Pinning in situ' with a single cannulated screw across the physis to stabilise the epiphysis and prevent further slip; severe/unstable slips → open reduction/realignment osteotomy in specialist hands (higher AVN risk with manipulation).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: When is prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip considered in SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Especially with an underlying endocrine disorder or young age (high bilateral risk).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the complications of SUFE?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (the major complication — much higher with unstable slips and forced reduction); chondrolysis (cartilage loss → stiffness); leg-length discrepancy, deformity, altered gait; premature osteoarthritis of the hip.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: A traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity — inflammation and micro-injury at the growth-plate/apophysis where the patellar tendon inserts into the top of the shin; one of the commonest causes of anterior knee pain in adolescents, especially active/sporty boys.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Why does Osgood-Schlatter disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: It is a benign, self-limiting overuse condition with a clinical diagnosis and conservative management; recognising it avoids unnecessary imaging and allows confident reassurance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Describe the core mechanism of Osgood-Schlatter disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: The patellar (quadriceps) tendon inserts into the tibial tuberosity, which in adolescence is still a growth plate (apophysis) — the weak link. During a growth spurt, repetitive forceful quadriceps pull (running, jumping, kicking) causes repeated micro-avulsions → inflammation and new bone growth → a visible/palpable lump; initially tender, then hard, non-tender and permanent as it heals.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the epidemiology of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Adolescents during the growth spurt — girls ~8–12, boys ~10–15 (slightly younger in girls); more common in boys and physically active children (jumping/sprinting sports); usually unilateral but can be bilateral (~20–30%).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the clinical features of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Gradual (insidious, atraumatic) onset; a visible/palpable, tender, hard lump over the tibial tuberosity (the classic sign); anterior knee pain; pain exacerbated by activity, kneeling and knee extension (resisted extension/squatting/stairs/running/jumping); relieved by rest; no systemic symptoms, no true joint effusion, knee otherwise normal (full range of movement).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: Where is tenderness localised in Osgood-Schlatter disease, and why does this matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: To the tibial tuberosity (not the joint line) — this helps distinguish it from intra-articular pathology.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: How is Osgood-Schlatter disease diagnosed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Clinically — the history and localised tuberosity tenderness are usually sufficient; no imaging needed in a typical case.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: When is X-ray used in Osgood-Schlatter disease, and what may it show?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude other pathology; a lateral knee X-ray may show fragmentation/irregularity or a separate ossicle at the tuberosity (changes overlap with normal, so confirmatory not required).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What red flags should prompt considering alternatives to Osgood-Schlatter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, effusion, or non-tuberosity pain → exclude infection, malignancy (osteosarcoma around the knee), juvenile idiopathic arthritis, patellar tendinopathy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the key management message for Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Reassurance — it is self-limiting and settles as the growth plate fuses (skeletal maturity).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the initial management of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Reduction/modification of physical activity (relative rest from aggravating sports — not complete inactivity), ice after activity, NSAIDs/simple analgesia.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What management follows once Osgood-Schlatter symptoms settle?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Stretching and physiotherapy — quadriceps/hamstring stretching and strengthening to offload the tuberosity; protective knee pads for kneeling; occasionally a short period of reduced loading.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What is the outcome of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Symptoms fully resolve over time (months–up to ~2 years), typically leaving a painless hard bony lump at the tuberosity.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.front: What are the rare complications of Osgood-Schlatter disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Orth.back: Complete avulsion fracture (the tuberosity separates from the tibia) → needs surgery; rarely a persistent painful ossicle in skeletally mature patients may warrant excision.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What two childhood-specific seizure disorders are covered in this topic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Infantile spasms (a serious epileptic encephalopathy) and febrile convulsions (common, usually benign).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the organising principle for paediatric seizures?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Age + context: infantile spasms (~4–8 mo; clusters of flexion spasms, developmental regression, hypsarrhythmia on EEG) is serious; febrile convulsion (6mo–5yr; brief generalised seizure with fever, normal neurology) is common and benign.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Give the clue and management for infantile spasms (West syndrome).
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Clusters of flexion 'salaam' spasms, regression; hypsarrhythmia → vigabatrin/ACTH; poor prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Give the clue and management for febrile convulsion.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: 6mo–5yr with fever; simple (brief, generalised) vs complex → reassure, antipyretics; small increased epilepsy risk if complex.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What makes a febrile convulsion 'complex', and what does it prompt?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Focal, prolonged (>15 min) or recurrent within 24h → further assessment; always exclude meningitis/encephalitis if unwell.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is West syndrome (infantile spasms)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A severe, age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy (now also called infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, IESS).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why does West syndrome matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: It is a paediatric neurological emergency in disguise — the spasms are easily mistaken for colic, reflux or startle, yet delayed treatment worsens the already-serious developmental outcome.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the classic triad defining West syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: (1) Epileptic (infantile) spasms — the 'salaam attacks'; (2) hypsarrhythmia on EEG — chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern; (3) developmental stagnation or regression — loss/plateau of skills.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the typical onset age of infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: 4–8 months (peak 3–7 months; almost always <1–2 years); slight male predominance.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What proportion of infantile spasms have an identifiable cause, and why does it matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: ~70–75% have an identifiable underlying cause ('symptomatic') — the brain insult matters for prognosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Which classic condition causes infantile spasms and changes treatment?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Tuberous sclerosis complex — vigabatrin is especially effective here.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: List causes of infantile spasms.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Tuberous sclerosis complex, structural/malformations (cortical dysplasia, lissencephaly), hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, congenital infection, Down syndrome, metabolic disorders, genetic (ARX, CDKL5); 'cryptogenic/idiopathic' (no cause found — better prognosis).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Describe 'salaam attacks'.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A sudden flexion of the head, trunk and arms, then extension of the arms (like the 'salaam' greeting; also 'jack-knife' spasms). Each spasm is brief (1–2 seconds) but occurs in CLUSTERS — repeated up to ~50 times, typically on waking/drifting off to sleep.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How do you distinguish infantile spasms from infantile colic?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: In colic the baby is distressed DURING the episodes; in infantile spasms the baby is often distressed/unsettled BETWEEN the spasms (and may cry after a cluster). If in doubt, do an EEG.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the key EEG finding in West syndrome?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Hypsarrhythmia — chaotic, high-voltage, disorganised slow waves and multifocal spikes. An urgent/sleep EEG is needed.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What imaging and cause work-up are done in infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: MRI brain (structural cause — malformation, tuberous sclerosis tubers, HIE); examine skin for tuberous sclerosis signs (ash-leaf macules under Wood's lamp, shagreen patch); metabolic/genetic work-up; TORCH screen.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is first-line drug treatment for infantile spasms, and its key caveat?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Vigabatrin — a GABAergic anticonvulsant; the drug of choice especially in tuberous sclerosis. Caveat: risk of irreversible peripheral visual field loss (retinal toxicity) — needs monitoring.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the role of corticosteroids in infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: High-dose oral prednisolone (or ACTH) — used first-line either alone or combined with vigabatrin (UK practice often uses combination hormonal therapy + vigabatrin, e.g. the ICISS approach); hormonal therapy gives faster short-term spasm control, long-term outcomes similar.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why avoid steroids as first-line in tuberous sclerosis-related infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Because vigabatrin is especially effective in tuberous sclerosis — a classic distinction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How are refractory infantile spasms managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Other anticonvulsants, ketogenic diet, or epilepsy surgery (for a focal structural cause). Refer urgently to paediatric neurology.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the prognosis of infantile spasms?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Generally poor — most children have long-term intellectual disability and ongoing epilepsy (may evolve into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome). Depends on cause: cryptogenic/idiopathic + prompt treatment = better; symptomatic (structural/tuberous sclerosis) = worse. Early recognition and treatment improve outcomes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A seizure triggered by a fever in a young child, WITHOUT any central-nervous-system infection or other identifiable neurological cause.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Why do febrile convulsions matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: They are the commonest seizure disorder of childhood (~3%); usually benign and self-limiting (so the skill is reassurance and safety-netting), but the fever means you must exclude a serious cause — especially meningitis/encephalitis — before attributing the seizure to a simple febrile convulsion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Describe the core concept of febrile convulsions.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: The immature brain has a low seizure threshold, and a rapidly rising temperature (during an intercurrent viral illness) tips it over → a seizure. It requires the fever to be from outside the CNS (e.g. viral URTI, tonsillitis, otitis media) — a seizure with fever from meningitis is NOT a febrile convulsion.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the definition/epidemiology of a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A seizure provoked by fever in an otherwise normal/neurologically healthy child, age 6 months–5 years (peak ~18 months), with no CNS infection, no metabolic cause and no history of afebrile seizures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a simple febrile convulsion defined?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Duration <15 min, generalised (tonic-clonic), no recurrence within 24h/same illness, complete recovery within <1 hour.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a complex febrile convulsion defined?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Any one of: >15 min, focal features, or recurring within 24h/the same febrile illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is febrile status epilepticus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A febrile seizure lasting >30 minutes (prolonged/continuous).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What are the typical clinical features of a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Occurs early in a viral illness as the temperature rapidly rises; usually brief (<5 minutes); mostly generalised tonic-clonic; a post-ictal period of drowsiness then complete recovery (in simple febrile convulsion); often a family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the priority in assessing a child with a febrile seizure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Find the source of the fever and EXCLUDE serious infection — especially meningitis/encephalitis (and pneumonia, UTI, etc.); use the NICE traffic-light system to risk-stratify.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: When should you have a low threshold for lumbar puncture in a febrile seizure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: In the very young (<18 months, especially <12 months) — meningeal signs are hard to elicit and a febrile seizure can be the presenting feature of meningitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Are routine investigations needed for a typical simple febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: No routine investigations in a well child with an obvious infection source; investigate as directed by the illness.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: When should a child with a febrile convulsion be admitted/referred to paediatrics?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: First febrile convulsion; complex features (>15 min, focal, or recurrent in the same illness); child <18 months; diagnostic uncertainty; suspected serious infection (e.g. meningitis); or the child appears unwell/incomplete recovery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: How is a prolonged febrile seizure (>5 minutes) managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: A rescue benzodiazepine — buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam (as per APLS/status epilepticus pathway).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Who initiates home rescue benzodiazepines for febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Only a specialist — for children with prolonged seizures/high recurrence risk/poor access to care.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: Do antipyretics prevent febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: No — antipyretics (paracetamol/ibuprofen) are for comfort only; they do NOT prevent febrile convulsions. No routine prophylactic anti-epileptic drugs (benign condition; adverse effects outweigh benefit).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the recurrence rate of febrile convulsions?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: ~1 in 3 (30%) will have another; recurrence risk factors: younger age at onset (<18 months), lower fever/shorter fever before seizure, family history.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What is the epilepsy risk after a febrile convulsion?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Very low — after a simple febrile convulsion the risk is only slightly above the general population (~1–2% baseline → ~2–7%); higher after complex febrile convulsion (and with family history of epilepsy, neurodevelopmental abnormality, or complex features).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.front: What seizure first aid should be taught to parents?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Seiz.back: Protect from injury, recovery position, time the seizure, don't restrain or put anything in the mouth, and call an ambulance if the seizure lasts >5 minutes, or there are repeated seizures, breathing difficulty, or the child doesn't recover.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What does the paediatric surgical GI topic cover?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The paediatric surgical abdomen — causes of obstruction, bilious vomiting and acute abdominal pain needing prompt surgical assessment.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the organising principle for the paediatric surgical abdomen?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Age + vomiting character + stool: bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate = malrotation/volvulus until proven otherwise; non-bilious projectile at 4–6 wks = pyloric stenosis; colicky pain + redcurrant-jelly stool 6mo–2yr = intussusception.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: 6mo–2yr; colicky pain, redcurrant-jelly stool, sausage mass; air/contrast enema ± surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: 4–6 wks; non-bilious projectile vomiting, olive mass, hypochloraemic alkalosis; pyloromyotomy.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for malrotation/volvulus.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Neonate/infant; bilious vomiting; upper-GI contrast; emergency Ladd's procedure.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the age and clue for Hirschsprung's disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Neonate; delayed meconium (>48h), distension; rectal biopsy (absent ganglia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Give the clue for Meckel's diverticulum and mesenteric adenitis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Meckel's: 'rule of 2s', painless PR bleeding, technetium scan. Mesenteric adenitis: post-viral, mimics appendicitis, self-limiting (exclusion).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The telescoping ('invagination') of one segment of bowel into the adjacent distal segment — the proximal bowel (intussusceptum) slides into the lumen ahead of it (intussuscipiens).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does intussusception matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction in infants/young children (6 months–2 years) and a surgical emergency — untreated, the trapped bowel's blood supply is cut off → ischaemia, necrosis, perforation and peritonitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The bowel telescopes → the mesentery is dragged in → venous compression → oedema and congestion → the bowel weeps blood and mucus (redcurrant jelly stool) → if unrelieved, arterial supply is compromised → ischaemia/gangrene/perforation.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the commonest anatomical type of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ileocolic (~90%) — the ileum invaginates through the ileocaecal valve into the colon.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the usual cause of intussusception in infants?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Mostly idiopathic — often follows a viral illness → hypertrophied Peyer's patches/lymphoid hyperplasia in the terminal ileum act as the lead point (rotavirus/adenovirus links).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When should you suspect a pathological lead point in intussusception, and what are the causes?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: With older age (>2–3 yr) or recurrence. Causes: Meckel's diverticulum (classic), intestinal polyp, duplication cyst, Henoch-Schönlein purpura (intramural haematoma), lymphoma (e.g. Burkitt's), cystic fibrosis (inspissated stool), post-op, tumours.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the classic pain pattern of intussusception.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Sudden, severe, paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain — episodes every ~15–20 min; the child draws the knees/legs up, screams, goes pale, then appears well/settled between episodes.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does vomiting evolve in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Initially non-bilious/reflex; becomes bilious as obstruction develops (bilious vomiting in a child = surgical until proven otherwise).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is 'redcurrant jelly' stool and its timing?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Blood + mucus — a LATE sign of intussusception; don't wait for it.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What abdominal signs occur in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A palpable 'sausage-shaped' mass (typically right upper quadrant/along the colon) with emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Dance's sign).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the atypical/apathetic presentation of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Lethargy — may be the sole or dominant feature (a lethargic, pale infant 'as if drugged'; ~15% present without the colic phase).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How often is the classic triad of intussusception present?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: In <25% of cases (colicky pain + redcurrant jelly stool + sausage mass) — so a high index of suspicion is needed; don't wait for all three.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the investigation of choice for intussusception and its findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ultrasound — shows the 'target'/'doughnut' sign (concentric rings on transverse view) or 'pseudokidney' sign (longitudinal).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What may abdominal X-ray show in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Not diagnostic, but may show signs of obstruction (distended loops, paucity of gas in right iliac fossa), a soft-tissue mass, or free air (perforation → contraindicates enema).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Resuscitate first — 'drip and suck': IV fluids (often dehydrated/shocked), NG tube for decompression, analgesia, and involve paediatric surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the first-line non-operative treatment for intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Air (pneumatic) enema (or contrast enema) under radiological guidance — both diagnostic AND therapeutic (~80–90% success) in a stable child.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When is an enema contraindicated in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Peritonitis, perforation, or haemodynamic instability/shock → straight to surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: When is surgery indicated in intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: If the enema fails, there's perforation/peritonitis/shock, or a pathological lead point is found → operative reduction ± bowel resection (if gangrenous); antibiotics if perforation/peritonitis suspected.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the recurrence rate after enema reduction of intussusception?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: ~5–10% (usually within 24–48h); recurrent episodes raise suspicion of a lead point.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle → gastric outlet obstruction in an infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is pyloric stenosis a classic exam scenario?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A firstborn baby boy with projectile NON-bilious vomiting at a few weeks old, and a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (the most-examined paediatric biochemistry); and it is NOT a surgical emergency — correct fluids/electrolytes first, then operate.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The pyloric muscle progressively hypertrophies → narrows/obstructs the gastric outlet → the stomach can't empty → forceful (projectile) vomiting of gastric contents only (non-bilious — the obstruction is proximal to the bile duct). Persistent vomiting of HCl drives the biochemical picture.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the age and demographics of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Presents at ~2–8 weeks (peak 3–6 weeks) — well at birth, then progressive vomiting; boys ~4:1, especially firstborn males; positive family history (especially maternal); associated with maternal smoking.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Projectile, NON-bilious vomiting — forceful, shortly after feeds.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What behaviour of the infant helps distinguish pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The baby remains HUNGRY and eager to feed again ('hungry vomiter') — unlike an unwell/septic infant.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is found on examination during a 'test feed' in pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A palpable, firm, non-tender 'OLIVE'-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant/epigastrium (the hypertrophied pylorus) + visible peristalsis (left-to-right waves after a feed).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the biochemical picture of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — with paradoxical aciduria (↓Cl⁻, ↓potassium, ↑bicarbonate, alkalotic pH, acidic urine).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain how vomiting causes the metabolic alkalosis in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Vomiting loses HCl → loss of H⁺ and Cl⁻ → ↓Cl⁻ (hypochloraemia) + ↑bicarbonate → metabolic alkalosis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain the hypokalaemia in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Volume depletion → the kidney activates RAAS/aldosterone → retains sodium and water but excretes potassium → ↓potassium (hypokalaemia).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Explain 'paradoxical aciduria' in pyloric stenosis.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Despite systemic alkalosis, once potassium is depleted the kidney is forced to excrete H⁺ (instead of potassium) to reabsorb sodium → the urine becomes acidic despite the blood being alkaline.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the investigation of choice for pyloric stenosis and its criteria?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ultrasound — shows pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm and pyloric channel length >15–17 mm. Venous/capillary blood gas + U&Es identify and quantify the alkalosis and guide fluid correction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is pyloric stenosis NOT an immediate surgical emergency?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Operating on an alkalotic, hypokalaemic baby risks post-op apnoea/arrhythmia and anaesthetic danger — resuscitate and correct fluids/electrolytes first.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Stop oral feeds, pass an NG tube (decompress/aspirate); IV fluid resuscitation + correct electrolytes — typically 0.9% saline with added potassium (± dextrose); monitor gas/U&Es until alkalosis and potassium/chloride normalise.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the definitive treatment of pyloric stenosis?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy — surgical division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle (down to but not through the mucosa), open or laparoscopic; excellent prognosis, feeds restart within hours–a day post-op.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is intestinal malrotation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A congenital abnormality of the position and fixation of the gut, from failure of the normal rotation of the midgut during fetal development.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does malrotation matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It leaves the bowel anchored on a dangerously narrow mesenteric base, predisposing to midgut volvulus — the whole midgut twisting around the superior mesenteric artery → a surgical emergency: the twist strangles the artery → rapid ischaemia and necrosis of the entire small bowel within hours (short-bowel syndrome or death).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the embryology behind malrotation.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Normally the midgut undergoes a 270° anticlockwise rotation around the SMA and fixes the duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure to the left of midline and the caecum in the right iliac fossa (a broad, stable mesenteric base). In malrotation this is incomplete → the caecum ends up high/midline, the DJ flexure is malpositioned, and the mesentery has a narrow pedicle → the bowel can twist, and Ladd's bands stretch across and obstruct the duodenum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What conditions are associated with malrotation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Exomphalos (omphalocele), congenital diaphragmatic hernia, intrinsic duodenal atresia; also gastroschisis, heterotaxy/situs abnormalities & congenital heart disease.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the cardinal red flag of malrotation/volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bilious (green) vomiting — from duodenal obstruction (Ladd's bands or the volvulus twist), which is distal to the ampulla → bile-stained.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the late/ischaemic signs of volvulus with strangulation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Abdominal tenderness/peritonism, PR bleeding (haematochezia), a distended tense abdomen, and shock — indicating bowel ischaemia → emergency.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How can malrotation present in older children?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Chronic intermittent bilious vomiting, recurrent abdominal pain, or failure to thrive (intermittent volvulus/Ladd's band obstruction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is THE rule about bilious vomiting in a neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bilious vomiting in a neonate = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. (Contrast pyloric stenosis = non-bilious projectile vomiting.)

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for malrotation and its findings?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Upper GI contrast study — shows the DJ flexure malpositioned (not left of midline) and, in volvulus, the pathognomonic 'corkscrew' appearance of the twisted duodenum/proximal jejunum.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What ultrasound sign indicates volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The 'whirlpool sign' — the superior mesenteric vein and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the SMA; may show the artery/vein relationship inverted.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What might abdominal X-ray show in malrotation, and what is the caveat?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Often non-specific; may show a 'double bubble' ± distal gas (duodenal obstruction) or a gasless abdomen (concerning). Not diagnostic. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging in an unstable/ill child with suspected volvulus.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of midgut volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Resuscitate (IV fluids, NG decompression, correct electrolytes, broad-spectrum antibiotics) and urgent paediatric surgery.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What are the steps of Ladd's procedure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Detorse the volvulus (untwist, usually anticlockwise); divide Ladd's bands (relieve duodenal obstruction); broaden the mesenteric base (prevent re-twisting); place small bowel on the right, caecum/colon on the left (non-rotated position); appendicectomy; resect any necrotic/gangrenous bowel (± second-look laparotomy).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why is appendicectomy done during Ladd's procedure?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The repositioned caecum would make future appendicitis present atypically.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How is asymptomatic (incidental) malrotation managed?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Usually elective Ladd's procedure (~15–20% lifetime volvulus risk), individualised.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the feared complication of malrotation with volvulus?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Bowel ischaemia/necrosis → short-bowel syndrome (if extensive resection needed); also perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, death (untreated volvulus).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal bowel — the nerves that drive peristalsis fail to develop, so the affected segment can't relax or propel stool → functional bowel obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does Hirschsprung's disease matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: It is a key cause of failure to pass meconium/neonatal bowel obstruction, the classic delayed meconium (>48 h) + distension + bilious vomiting scenario, strongly associated with Down syndrome, and its complication HAEC can be life-threatening.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of Hirschsprung's disease.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: During embryogenesis, neural crest cells migrate craniocaudally down the gut to form the enteric nervous system (Meissner submucosal and Auerbach myenteric plexuses). In Hirschsprung's this migration stops short → the distal bowel has NO ganglion cells → the aganglionic segment is tonically contracted/unable to relax → functional obstruction → the proximal bowel dilates (megacolon), with a transition zone between them.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the extent and commonest form of aganglionosis in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Always distal and continuous from the anus proximally — ~75% is short-segment (rectosigmoid); rarely total colonic. Boys ~4:1.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What conditions and genes are associated with Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Strongly associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — also Waardenburg syndrome, MEN2, congenital central hypoventilation. The RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10) is the strongest genetic association; can be familial.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the classic red flag of Hirschsprung's disease in the neonate?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life (normally passed within 24–48 h).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the classic neonatal triad of Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and delayed meconium (neonatal distal bowel obstruction).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does Hirschsprung's present in older infants/children (short-segment)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Chronic severe constipation, abdominal distension, failure to thrive.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the 'squirt/blast sign' on PR examination in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A tight/empty rectum, then explosive passage of stool and gas when the finger is withdrawn (decompression of the obstructed proximal bowel).

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: How does Hirschsprung's contrast with functional constipation?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Hirschsprung's: from birth/delayed meconium, empty rectum on PR. Functional constipation: later onset, stool in the rectum, responds to laxatives.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: A life-threatening complication — inflammation/infection of the obstructed bowel: fever, explosive/foul diarrhoea, abdominal distension, sepsis; can → toxic megacolon and perforation. Can be the presenting feature; needs urgent resuscitation, IV antibiotics, rectal washouts/decompression.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Rectal (suction) biopsy — shows ABSENCE of ganglion cells in the submucosal/myenteric plexuses, with hypertrophied/thickened nerve fibres and increased acetylcholinesterase staining.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What do contrast enema and anorectal manometry show in Hirschsprung's?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Contrast (barium) enema — may show the transition zone (narrow aganglionic distal segment → dilated proximal colon); helps plan surgery but is not diagnostic alone. Anorectal manometry — absent recto-anal inhibitory reflex (the internal sphincter fails to relax); a screening adjunct. Abdominal X-ray shows distal obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the initial management of Hirschsprung's disease (obstructed/HAEC)?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Resuscitate, NG decompression, bowel/rectal washouts (to decompress and bridge to surgery), IV antibiotics if enterocolitis.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is the definitive treatment of Hirschsprung's disease?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Surgical 'pull-through' procedure — resect the aganglionic segment and anastomose normally innervated bowel to the anus (e.g. Soave, Swenson, Duhamel), often single-stage (± an initial defunctioning colostomy in sick/late cases). There are no effective medical cures.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: What is Meckel's diverticulum?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The commonest congenital anomaly of the GI tract — a true diverticulum of the distal ileum that is a remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Why does Meckel's diverticulum matter?
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: Although most are asymptomatic, it is the number-one cause of painless, massive lower-GI bleeding in young children, and it can mimic appendicitis or cause bowel obstruction.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: Describe the core mechanism of Meckel's diverticulum.
conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.back: The omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct connects the developing gut to the yolk sac and normally obliterates by ~week 7. Incomplete obliteration leaves a blind-ending pouch on the antimesenteric border of the ileum — a true diverticulum (all bowel-wall layers). It often contains ectopic gastric (± pancreatic) mucosa: the ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid → ulcerates adjacent ileal mucosa → painless bleeding.

conditions__PAEDIATRICS__Paediatric Surg.front: State the 'rule of 2s' for Meckel's diverticulum.
